result.cluster: ACE-Step 1.5: license, footprint, Apple Silicon, task matrix, quality (ace-step)

results.question: What license applies to each ACE-Step 1.5 component AURA would use: repo code, base, turbo, SFT and XL (base/SFT/turbo) DiT checkpoints, the LM planner checkpoints and the VAE? Are any weights under non-MIT or additional terms?
results.finding: Every ACE-Step 1.5 component is MIT and none of the HF repos is gated (checked 2026-10-09). The GitHub LICENSE is MIT, Copyright (c) 2026 ACEStep. The HF API returns license:mit and gated=False for all of these: Ace-Step1.5 (the main bundle: VAE, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, acestep-v15-turbo, acestep-5Hz-lm-1.7B), acestep-v15-base, acestep-v15-sft, acestep-v15-turbo-shift1, turbo-shift3, turbo-continuous, acestep-v15-xl-base, xl-sft, xl-turbo, the three official XL diffusers-format repos, acestep-5Hz-lm-0.6B, acestep-5Hz-lm-4B, ace-step-v1.5-1d-vae-stable-audio-format, acestep-captioner and acestep-transcriber. The VAE is ACE's own 1D Oobleck-architecture VAE. The paper says it was trained for 600k steps on 120 A100s; it is not Stability's weights. The card labels it MIT. Inherited terms: the LM checkpoints are fine-tunes of Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B and 4B. The bundled text encoder is the unmodified Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. All four Qwen models are Apache-2.0 on HF. The main ACE repo ships that encoder under an MIT tag with no LICENSE or NOTICE file, so redistributing AURA with the weights needs Apache-2.0 attribution for the Qwen parts. Non-MIT items in the ACE ecosystem: ACE-Step-v1.5-chinese-new-year-LoRA is CreativeML OpenRAIL-M, which carries use restrictions. The org's ACE-Step-DAW repo is AGPL-3.0. The old ACE-Step v1 (3.5B) is Apache-2.0. Community items: ScragVAE and the Serveurperso GGUFs are both MIT.
results.code_license: MIT (ace-step/ACE-Step-1.5). Org's ACE-Step-DAW is AGPL-3.0. acestep.cpp and acestep.vst3 are MIT.
results.weights_license: MIT, ungated, for all 1.5 DiT (2B and XL), LM, VAE, captioner and transcriber checkpoints. No revenue cap, non-commercial clause or gating. The LM is derived from Apache-2.0 Qwen3 and the bundled Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B is Apache-2.0, so keep Apache attribution when redistributing. The official CNY LoRA is OpenRAIL-M.
results.output_rights: The HF cards say 'You can strictly use the generated music for commercial purposes' and claim licensed, royalty-free/public-domain and MIDI-synthetic training data. That is a vendor claim: the paper does not list sources. The README disclaimer is non-binding responsible-use guidance: verify originality, disclose AI involvement, get permissions when adapting protected styles.

results.question: For each variant (2B base/turbo vs 4B XL), what are the documented VRAM or unified-memory requirements with and without offload or INT8, and the total download size per profile?
results.finding: VRAM, from the README, GPU_COMPATIBILITY.md and the gpu_config.py constants. The 2B DiT runs in 4GB or less only as 'Tier 1': DiT-only, no LM, INT8 plus full CPU offload, max 4 min (6 min without LM). The LM needs 6GB or more. bf16 weight constants: 2B DiT 4.7GB, XL DiT 9.0GB, VAE 0.33GB, text encoder 1.2GB, LM 0.6B/1.7B/4B at 1.2/3.4/8.0GB plus a 0.3-1.6GB KV cache. Activations per batch item: turbo 0.3GB, base 0.6GB, xl_turbo 0.5GB, xl_base 1.0GB. XL needs 12GB or more with offload plus INT8 (marginal), 16GB or more with CPU offload, 20GB or more without offload, and 24GB or more for XL plus the 4B LM. That matches gpt-sol-core and Kimi's '12-20GB'. The XL-SFT card wrongly labels its weights 'bf16 ~18.8 GB'. The safetensors header shows the native XL checkpoint is stored in F32: 4.99B params, total_size 19,949,242,904 bytes. It loads as bf16 at about 9GB, matching the README. Download sizes from the HF tree API, decimal GB: Ace-Step1.5 main bundle 10.09 (9.40 GiB) = turbo 4.79 + 1.7B LM 3.76 + Qwen3-Embedding 1.21 + VAE 0.34. Each 2B base/SFT/turbo variant is 4.79. Each native XL base/SFT/turbo is 19.95 (18.58 GiB) and also needs the main bundle's encoder and VAE. LM 0.6B is 1.37; LM 4B is 8.43. Official diffusers-format XL turbo is about 11.1 and XL SFT about 11.5, both self-contained bf16. Smallest official-weights profile, 2B turbo with no LM and selective download: about 6.34 GB (5.9 GiB). The default first-run download (10.09 GB) does not fit the Mac's 8.5 GiB free disk, before counting the Python environment. Community GGUFs (Serveurperso, MIT, for acestep.cpp): turbo Q8 2.55, XL Q8 5.31, XL Q4_K_M 2.99, 4B LM Q8 4.46, text encoder Q8 0.78.
results.hardware_notes: On MPS, gpu_config.py forces no INT8 (torchao unsupported), no CPU offload and no torch.compile, so the 4GB/INT8 figures do not apply to Mac. Full bf16 weights stay resident. My estimate from the vendor constants: XL + 4B LM ≈ 9+1.2+0.33+8+1.6 ≈ 20GB plus activations, which fits 48GB unified memory. Not measured. Whether the MLX conversion briefly holds both PyTorch and MLX copies is unverified.
results.corrected_value: The native XL download is about 19.95 GB per checkpoint (F32 on disk), not 9 GB. The default main bundle is 10.09 GB, more than the 8.5 GiB free. The 'less than 4GB' figure is CUDA-only (INT8 plus offload, DiT-only).

results.question: Is Apple Silicon (MLX and/or MPS) supported in upstream ACE-Step 1.5, or only in the 'clockworksquirrel' community fork? Which variants and tasks work on Mac, and is there any published Apple Silicon timing?
results.finding: Upstream supports Apple Silicon officially. The repo describes itself as 'supporting Mac, AMD, Intel, and CUDA'. It ships macOS launch scripts (start_gradio_ui_macos.sh, start_api_server_macos.sh) that set ACESTEP_LM_BACKEND=mlx, plus a macOS portable package. The code includes a native MLX DiT decoder and MLX VAE encode/decode (acestep/models/mlx/*, mlx_dit_init.py, mlx_vae_*), an MLX LM backend, and PyTorch MPS. The v0.1.6 release notes list MLX support for XL (#1002). v0.1.7 brought DCW on MLX and MLX VAE chunk auto-tuning. v0.1.8 added MLX repaint step-injection and boundary blend (#1197). INSTALL lists M1-M4. M5 Max 128GB users report XL running on the official tracker (issue #1259). Task availability is set per checkpoint, not per device: there is no Mac-specific task restriction, and vLLM is unavailable (pt/mlx only). Known Mac pitfall: xl-base and xl-sft produced garbled audio through the CLI/API because DCW defaults on. The fix landed in Gradio in v0.1.8 (#1207) and in CLI/API only on main after v0.1.8 (#1282, 2026-08-28); the workaround is dcw_enabled=False, shift=1.0. Upstream publishes no Apple Silicon timings, only the profile_inference.py --device mps tool. The fork clockworksquirrel/ace-step-apple-silicon (MIT, 5 stars, last push 2026-07-07) is a separate MPS/MLX-LM port with a Claude 'AI DJ' UI. It claims about 25s for a 30-second song (turbo, 8 steps) on an M3 Pro 36GB and about 1.5 min for SFT at 32 steps. Kimi's 'about 25s/song' misreads this: it is per 30-second clip, fork-claimed, and the fork is largely superseded by upstream native MLX. The lilting.ch article covers ACE-Step v1 (3.5B), not 1.5, so its M2 Max figures do not apply.
results.hardware_notes: Official: MLX for the LM, DiT and VAE, plus PyTorch MPS. Not officially listed but reported working on the official tracker: M5 Max. No official Mac speed figures; the only number is fork-claimed (M3 Pro 36GB, about 25s per 30s turbo clip). For M5 Pro 48GB, Phase 0 should run profile_inference.py --device mps --lm-backend mlx and record its own timings.
results.corrected_value: Upstream has native MLX and MPS. The clockworksquirrel fork is optional and not required. 25s is per 30-second clip on the fork, not per song.

results.question: Which tasks does each checkpoint support: text2music, cover, repaint, extend/complete, lego, extract (stems), and voice or timbre reference? How does turbo handle CFG and step count? Does any checkpoint support singer identity or timbre cloning?
results.finding: Task matrix, consistent across the README Model Zoo, INFERENCE.md, the HF cards and code constants.py. 2B base and xl-base support everything: text2music, cover (plus cover-nofsq 'raw remix'), repaint, extract, lego and complete. 2B SFT, 2B turbo (all shift variants), xl-sft and xl-turbo support text2music, cover/cover-nofsq and repaint only, with no extract, lego or complete. The Gradio UI enables Extract, Lego and Complete only for 'pure base' paths. ace_step_musicians_guide.md wrongly says 'base/SFT'. Definitions: 'Complete' adds accompaniment to a partial or single track (e.g. a cappella vocals). It is not time-extension. Time extension and continuation use Repaint at the start or end, in 3-90s regions, on all models. Extract is generative stem isolation into 12 track names (vocals, backing_vocals, drums, bass, guitar, keyboard, percussion, strings, synth, fx, brass, woodwinds). All six DiTs accept reference_audio, which acts as a global, time-averaged timbre, mix and performance-style condition. The paper describes a timbre encoder trained for 'zero-shot timbre cloning'. There is no dedicated singer-identity or speaker-embedding clone and no published identity metric, so singer cloning is unverified. Turbo: 8 steps by default (1-20 allowed; before v0.1.7 it was silently clamped to 8). guidance_scale is auto-corrected to 1.0 because turbo has no CFG. shift is not auto-set and must be set to 3.0 by hand. Base/SFT: 50 steps (32-64 recommended), CFG default 7.0 (typical 5-9); ADG is base-only. The LM is skipped for cover, repaint and extract, and used for text2music, lego and complete. Commit #1287 on main makes skip-LM the interim default for complete/lego. Post-v0.1.8 additions: retake_variance, flow_edit_morph (an overlay on cover), repaint_mode/repaint_strength, cover_noise_strength.
results.corrected_value: No single checkpoint does 'every primitive' at best quality. Stems, lego and complete need base or xl-base (lowest-quality tier). SFT and turbo, XL included, do text2music, cover and repaint only. Timbre reference is global and time-averaged, not a singer-identity clone.

results.question: What speed and duration figures are documented (under 10s per song on an RTX 3090, songs up to 10 minutes), and what are the current release features (Retake, Flow-Edit, repaint improvements, Docker)? What is the latest tagged release to pin?
results.finding: Speed and duration (vendor-claimed, not independently measured): the README and paper say under 2s per full song on an A100 and under 10s on an RTX 3090. The README adds 0.5-10s on an A100 depending on think mode and steps. The paper says 240s tracks in about 1s on an A100 with the 8-step distilled DiT. These figures predate XL and refer to the 2B turbo. Duration is 10-600s and batches go up to 8. Tier caps apply: 8 min with LM below 24GB, 10 min at 24GB or more. v0.1.8 (2026-05-18) adds: Retake (retake_variance 0-1, ported from 1.0); Flow-Edit (prompt-guided editing, redesigned as an overlay on Remix/cover); repaint improvements (cached source latents #1177, MLX step-injection and boundary blend #1197); a raw remix task (cover-nofsq); a generic Dockerfile with CI-built images at ghcr.io/ace-step/ace-step-1.5 (tags 0.1.8 and latest = dce6214). v0.1.7 added DCW and community VAE swap. v0.1.6 (2026-04-03) released XL. The vendor's 'XL best on all 11 metrics' has no published table. Latest tag: v0.1.8, commit dce621408bee8c31b4fcf4811682eb9359e1bc94. main is 21 commits ahead at HEAD ca1e85fe9430179831e6bc6be790c332190a3866 (2026-08-29). Those commits include #1282 (DCW off by default for non-turbo in CLI/API, fixing garbled XL-SFT/base output), #1292 (explicit repaint chunk mask), #1287 (skip-LM default for complete/lego), #1305 (neutralize cover-only params on non-cover tasks) and #1284 (on-demand model loading). The 'cloud XL turbo 14-second clips' roundup claim cannot be verified from primary sources and does not affect the pin.
results.hardware_notes: All speed numbers are vendor-claimed on CUDA (A100, 3090) for the 2B turbo. No XL or Apple Silicon timing is published.
results.corrected_value: Pin main ca1e85fe9 (or later), or pin v0.1.8 and set dcw_enabled=False and shift=1.0 explicitly for non-turbo (SFT/base) models.

results.question: What do ACE-Step's 39.1/26.3 vs Suno v5 46.8/34.2 numbers measure, and were they computed with ACE's own reward models? Does a third-party WildSongBench result of 6.01 vs Suno v5 6.87 exist?
results.finding: From paper Table 1 (arXiv 2602.00744v3): 39.1 and 26.3 are 'Style Align' and 'Lyric Align'. They are quantified with ACE's 'proprietary ACE-Caption-Reward and ACE-Lyric-Reward models', so they are self-scored. Suno v5 scored 46.8/34.2, Suno v4.5 40.5/32.7 and MiniMax-2.0 43.1/29.5. Setup: 1.7B LM plus dynamic distilled 2B DiT (no RL); a test set of 20 styles with zh/en prompts and lyrics generated by Gemini 3 Pro. On third-party AudioBox and SongEval, ACE 1.5 had the highest CU (8.09), second-best PQ (8.35) and tied-best Coherence (4.72). In the Music Arena human evaluation, the authors place it between Suno v4.5 and v5. WildSongBench exists: arXiv 2609.33757 (YuE2, M-A-P, 2026-09-27) and the HF dataset m-a-p/WildSongBench, 192 in-the-wild prompts. On SongBench Global Avg, ACE-Step 1.5 scores 6.0118 versus Suno v5 6.8721, Suno v6 6.5562, Suno v6 Wild 6.4195, Mureka 9 6.9377, and YuE2 6.7316 (6.9632 best-of-8). ACE has the second-lowest public-system PER, 0.0746. Caveats: the WSB authors are a competing model team, and the ACE variant used in WSB is not stated in the text (their cover test used XL-SFT). WSB postdates the paper and is the better external yardstick for a 'Suno v6-class' target.

results.question: What does the ACE-Step 1.5 report say about training data (6M stem-separated tracks vs about 20M pairs; licensed/PD/synthetic), and does a one-click LoRA trainer exist that trains on about 8 songs in about 1 hour on a 3090 or a 12GB card (and on Mac)?
results.finding: Data (paper sections 2 and 4): a 27M-sample annotated corpus. A 5M-sample golden set was annotated by Gemini 2.5 Pro and used to train ACE-Captioner and ACE-Transcriber (from Qwen2.5-Omni). 4M contrastive pairs trained the reward models. Curriculum: about 20M text-to-music pairs for foundation pre-training. The omni-task phase keeps the top 50% plus 6M stem-separated tracks; section 4 calls this the 17M-sample omni-task mixture. A final 2M high-quality SFT. The VAE was trained for 600k steps on 120 A100s. Kimi's 6M figure and gpt-sol-core's 20M figure are both in the paper. The paper does not state licensing or sources. 'Licensed + royalty-free/public domain + synthetic MIDI-to-audio' appears only on the HF model cards, so it is an unaudited vendor claim. LoRA: one-click annotation and training exists in the Gradio 'Train LoRA' tab, plus 'Train LoKr' and an API at /v1/training/start and start_lokr. The two official docs disagree on hardware. The README says '8 songs, 1 hour on 3090 (12GB VRAM)'. LoRA_Training_Tutorial.md says 16GB minimum, 20GB or more recommended, and 'VRAM usage typically stays around 17 GB'. It also says LoKr cuts 'an hour' to about 5 minutes. Mac: the trainer has MPS code paths (fp16 autocast, fp32 decoder weights; #1245 fixes fp32 on MPS). A 2026-09-22 report on M5 Max, on closed issue #619, describes all-NaN gradients from the fp16 text encoder on MPS and offers a patch. No official Mac training timing exists, and the fix is unverified upstream. XL LoRA support arrived in v0.1.6.
results.hardware_notes: LoRA VRAM: README says 12GB on a 3090; the tutorial says 16GB minimum and about 17GB typical. Both are vendor statements. Mac LoRA: code path exists, with a community-reported NaN bug on M5 Max MPS in Sept 2026. Treat it as untested.
results.corrected_value: Both data figures are correct: about 20M pre-training pairs, and 6M stem-separated tracks added in the omni-task phase, within a 27M corpus. The licensing claim is card-only. Plan LoRA VRAM at 16-20GB, not 12GB, and prefer LoKr.

results.question: Can ACE-Step cover or audio-to-audio conditioning follow a hummed or sung melody (pitch contour and timing) when making a full song? What strength or parameters control adherence, and what other melody-conditioned options exist (MusicGen-melody license, MIDI-conditioned engines)?
results.finding: ACE mechanism, per the vendor: Cover (task 'cover') quantizes src_audio into 5Hz FSQ semantic codes. The Tutorial says these carry 'Melody: note direction and pitch', rhythm, chords, orchestration and some timbre. The paper says quantized latents preserve 'melody and rhythm'. Adherence controls: audio_cover_strength (0-1; 1.0 strong, 0.5 balanced, 0.1 loose; 0.2 suggested for style transfer); cover_noise_strength (0 = start from pure noise, 1 = closest to source); task 'cover-nofsq' (raw remix without FSQ, v0.1.8); flow_edit_morph overlay; caption and lyrics. The LM is skipped for cover. Complete and Lego (base/xl-base only) can build accompaniment around a single sung or a cappella track, but they keep that track rather than re-singing it. ACE has no MIDI or symbolic input. No vendor doc or evaluation covers hummed input. Contrary evidence: in YuE2's SHS100K cover test (third party, competitor-authored), ACE-Step 1.5 XL-SFT in native cover mode reached only CLEWS Hit@1 2.4% and mAP 0.024. Settings were strength 0.8, noise 0, 50 steps, CFG 7, shift 3, thinking off. SongEcho reached 48.4% Hit@1, meaning ACE covers poorly preserved work identity. Hum-following therefore has to be measured in Phase 0. Alternatives: MusicGen-melody does chroma conditioning; code MIT, weights CC-BY-NC-4.0, so non-commercial. Meta JASCO (chords, drums, melody) is CC-BY-NC-4.0 and manually gated. YuE2-3B (2026-09-27) takes a user ABC score (melody-only 'cot=melody' mode for covers) and is the closest open fit for a hum→transcription→score→song path. Its weights are CC-BY-NC-4.0, code Apache-2.0, and it needs Linux plus a 24GB NVIDIA GPU. SongEcho conditions on vocal melody; its license was not verified. Spotify Basic Pitch (Apache-2.0) handles audio→MIDI. Suno Studio supports 'MIDI clips ... as a prompt' (blog, 2026-08-13), but it is commercial and closed.
results.weights_license: ACE: MIT. MusicGen-melody: CC-BY-NC-4.0. JASCO: CC-BY-NC-4.0, manually gated. YuE2-3B, YuE2-Vae and SheetSage2: CC-BY-NC-4.0. Basic Pitch: Apache-2.0.
results.output_rights: ACE outputs are claimed commercial-OK. Outputs of any CC-BY-NC model (MusicGen-melody, JASCO, YuE2) are not safe for LLC or commercial release.
results.corrected_value: Vendor docs say cover keeps melody, but third-party measurement shows weak melody and identity retention at strength 0.8. Treat 'ACE cover at high strength on the hum' as an unvalidated hypothesis. Test strength 0.9-1.0, cover_noise_strength and cover-nofsq on real hums before committing.

new_discoveries: YuE2 (arXiv 2609.33757, 2026-09-27; HF m-a-p/YuE2-3B, about 7.3 GB). It plans a readable melody and chord ABC score before rendering audio and accepts a user-supplied ABC score; cot='melody' is the recommended cover mode. That fits hum → Basic Pitch or SheetSage2 → ABC → full song better than ACE cover. WildSongBench: 6.73, or 6.96 best-of-8, against Suno v5 at 6.87. Limits: weights CC-BY-NC-4.0 (YuE2-3B, YuE2-Vae, SheetSage2, MERT2), code Apache-2.0, Linux plus a 24GB BF16 NVIDIA GPU. Personal non-commercial use only.

WildSongBench ranks Suno v6 (6.56) and v6 Wild (6.42) below Suno v5 (6.87) on SongBench Global Avg; Mureka 9 is highest among the proprietary systems at 6.94. The owner's 'Suno 6.5' target needs an operational definition: choose a benchmark and a listening protocol.

DCW defaults to on and garbles xl-sft and xl-base output (issue #1259, reproduced on M5 Max via MLX and MPS). Gradio was fixed in v0.1.8 (#1207). The CLI/API fix (#1282) exists only on main after v0.1.8. Pin main ca1e85fe9 or later, or force dcw_enabled=False and shift=1.0 for non-turbo models.

Native XL checkpoints are stored in F32 (19.95 GB each). The XL-SFT card's 'bf16 ~18.8 GB' label is wrong. Official diffusers-format XL repos are bf16 and self-contained at about 11.1-11.5 GB. AceStepPipeline is merged into huggingface/diffusers but needs a source install. Whether the upstream ACE-Step app loads diffusers-format weights is unverified.

The default first-run download (Ace-Step1.5 main bundle, 10.09 GB / 9.40 GiB) exceeds the Mac's 8.5 GiB free disk. Free space, point ACESTEP_CHECKPOINTS_DIR at an external volume, or download selectively (turbo, encoder and VAE only is about 6.34 GB).

acestep.cpp (C++17/GGML) and acestep.vst3 sit in the ace-step org but were written by community member ServeurpersoCom; both MIT. They run on Metal, CUDA, Vulkan and CPU. The README says the docs cover all six tasks; LoRA is supported. Community GGUFs (MIT): turbo Q8 2.55 GB, XL Q4_K_M 2.99 GB, XL Q8 5.31 GB. This is a much smaller Mac footprint plus a DAW plugin, but it is a third-party quantization whose quality is unmeasured.
The org's ACE-Step-DAW repo is AGPL-3.0. Do not copy its code into AURA if AURA might be closed or permissively licensed.

Third-party cover-identity test (YuE2, SHS100K): ACE-Step 1.5 XL-SFT native cover reached Hit@1 2.4% versus SongEcho's 48.4% (arXiv 2602.19976, vocal-melody-conditioned cover; license unverified). AURA's melody path cannot assume ACE cover preserves a hummed tune.

The ACE LM checkpoints are Qwen3 fine-tunes, and the bundled text encoder is Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Apache-2.0) shipped under an MIT tag with no NOTICE file. Redistributing AURA with weights needs Apache-2.0 attribution.

LoRA on Mac: a 2026-09-22 report on M5 Max (comment on closed issue #619) describes all-NaN gradients from the fp16 text encoder on MPS, with a patch offered. The upstream fix is unconfirmed. The official LoRA tutorial also contradicts the README: 16GB minimum and about 17GB typical, versus 12GB. Prefer LoKr, which the docs say cuts about 1 hour to about 5 minutes.

Extract, Lego and Complete exist only on base and xl-base, the lower-quality, high-diversity tier. A stem workflow on ACE means loading a second large checkpoint (xl-base is another 19.95 GB on disk), or using a dedicated separator instead.
acestep-v15-turbo-rl is still 'To be released' on the HF card. The latest tag is v0.1.8 (2026-05-18); Docker images are at ghcr.io/ace-step/ace-step-1.5:0.1.8 and :latest (dce6214).
Suno Studio now accepts MIDI clips as generation prompts (suno.com/blog/studio-2, 2026-08-13). That is the commercial reference point for MIDI-conditioned generation, which ACE lacks.

results.question: Owner hardware inventory: Linux and Windows CPU, RAM, GPU, VRAM, driver/CUDA, free disk and network; Mac free disk (~8.5 GiB) and whether an external or cleaned volume can hold engine weights.
results.finding:
The Linux and Windows specs could not be checked. Neither machine can be reached from this Mac: `tailscale status` lists only two macOS nodes, `~/.ssh/config` lists only Mac hosts, and `nvidia-smi` is not installed here. The owner has to run the inventory on each box: `nvidia-smi`, `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,driver_version,compute_cap --format=csv`, `lscpu`, `free -h` and `df -h` on Linux, and `dxdiag` or `nvidia-smi` on Windows. Mac, checked locally on 2026-10-09:
- MacBook Pro Mac17,8 with an Apple M5 Pro: 18 CPU cores (6 Super + 12 Performance), 20-core GPU, Metal 4, 48 GB unified memory.
- macOS is 26.6.2 (build 25G83), not plain 26.6.
- Free space on the Data volume is 5.5 GiB, not ~8.5 GiB (926 GiB volume, 851 GiB used, 100% capacity).

An external volume is already mounted: "/Volumes/Backup Plus". It is a 2.0 TB USB drive (media name "BUP Slim"), formatted exFAT, with 1.2 TiB free, and a test file wrote successfully.
- exFAT has no symlinks. Hugging Face's cache docs say the cache then stores files directly in snapshots/ in a "degraded version" that can download a file several times. Set HF_HOME or HF_HUB_CACHE to that volume, and optionally HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS=1.
- The "BUP Slim" name suggests a Seagate Backup Plus Slim, which is usually a spinning drive. diskutil reports SSD status as unavailable. Load speed was not measured.

Possible space to reclaim (read-only `du`; the owner decides, nothing was deleted): ~/.ollama 21G, ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator 16G, Xcode simulator runtimes 11.6G (iOS 26.5 + watchOS 26.5 images), ~/Library/Caches 6.6G, ~/.cache/uv 3.3G. That is about 58 GB.

Weight sizes from the Hugging Face API (decimal GB):
- ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5: 10.09 GB. Each XL variant (xl-sft, xl-turbo, xl-base) adds 19.95 GB.
- YuE2-3B: 7.30 GB, plus YuE2-Vae 0.53 and SheetSage2 0.23.
- MiniMax-Music3: 57.35 GB (53.41 GiB) for the full repo. The diffusers components alone come to about 28.5 GB (see new_discoveries).
- Shao-MusicGeneration-v1.0: 52.21 GB.
- HeartMuLa-oss-3B: 15.75 GB.
- TTS: OmniVoice 3.27, Qwen3-TTS-1.7B 4.54, chatterbox-turbo 4.04, Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B 9.75, Kokoro-82M 0.36.

Conclusion: nothing beyond a TTS model fits on the Mac's internal disk today. The external exFAT volume can hold every engine. A ~58 GB cleanup would fit ACE base + XL plus TTS internally. results.question: Recompute cost per song and per accepted song from measured RTF; does $0.01-0.03 per song hold with best-of-n 8-16 and acceptance rates? Does 'under $15/mo at 500 songs' hold?
results.finding:
No RTF has been measured on the owner's hardware or on a rental. The figures below come from vendor speed claims and one community benchmark, multiplied by the verified 2026-10-09 prices from cost-2. All are warm-worker compute costs only. Each session adds billed model-load time, plus 5 s idle on RunPod or 60 s on Modal.

**Per-candidate cost:**
- ACE-Step 1.5 turbo. The vendor claims "under 10s on an RTX 3090" per full song. That works out to about $0.0019 per candidate on RunPod's 24GB serverless tier ($0.69/hr) and $0.0031 on the 4090 PRO tier. XL and thinking mode are slower and unmeasured.
- YuE2. The vendor table gives "A 3.6-minute song in 71 seconds on an RTX 4090" (RTF about 0.33). That is about $0.0217 per candidate on RunPod serverless 4090 and $0.0089 on a Vast 4090 at the median rate.
- MiniMax-Music3. No official speed is published. A community audio.cpp benchmark on an RTX 5090 gives RTF 0.74 (Q4/Q8) to 1.39 (BF16) for a 30-s clip. A 3.5-min song would then take 155-292 s: $0.068-0.128 per candidate on RunPod serverless 5090 ($1.58/hr) or $0.033-0.063 on a Vast 5090.

**Per brief (n candidates), compute only:**

| Engine | 2 candidates | 8 candidates | 16 candidates |
|---|---|---|---|
| ACE (RunPod serverless) | $0.004-0.006 | | $0.03-0.05 |
| YuE2 (RunPod serverless / Vast) | $0.043 / $0.018 | $0.17 / $0.07 | $0.35 / $0.14 |
| MiniMax (RunPod serverless) | | $0.54-1.03 | $1.09-2.05 |

Per accepted song = (candidates generated per accepted song) x (per-candidate cost) + model-load overhead + human review time. The acceptance rate is unknown, so GPT's $0.2667 per accepted brief stays hypothetical. It is in line with YuE2 at roughly best-of-12 on RunPod serverless 4090.

**Verdict on Kimi's claims:**
- "$0.01-0.03 per song" holds only for ACE-class or YuE2 at 2 variants.
- "Under $0.20 per song for best-of-n" holds for ACE at any n and for YuE2 up to about best-of-8 on serverless. It fails for YuE2 best-of-16 ($0.35) and for MiniMax at any n of 8 or more.
- "Under $15/mo at 500 songs" holds only if the burst tier averages $0.03 per song or less. That means ACE-class rendering, Mac drafts with about one heavy-engine render per song, or Vast pods with no idle time.

For comparison at 500 songs/month:
- YuE2 best-of-8 costs about $87/mo on RunPod serverless or $36 on Vast.
- MiniMax best-of-8 costs about $135-515/mo.
- Keeping about 100 GB of weights on a RunPod network volume adds about $7/mo. Modal includes 1 TiB of volume storage free, and its $30/mo Starter credit would cover the ACE and YuE2 tiers.

The Mac's electricity cost was not computed.

results.question: CUDA stack constraints per engine (torch cu126 vs cu128, Blackwell sm_120, flash-attn pins, Shao NGC pin, MiniMax Diffusers PR pin); which engines run on the owner's GPU generation and on Windows?
results.finding:
**PyTorch.** The current release is 2.14.1 (2026-09-30).
- Per RELEASE.md, the 2.14 stable CUDA wheels are cu126, cu130 and cu132.
- The cu126 wheels cover Maxwell through Hopper with no Blackwell. The cu130 and cu132 wheels cover Turing through Blackwell (10.0, 12.0+PTX).
- On download.pytorch.org, the last cu128 wheel is torch 2.11.0 and the last cu129 wheel is torch 2.13.0.
- The 2.9-era table lists cu128 as covering Volta through Blackwell (10.0, 12.0).
- The default PyPI wheel for torch 2.14.1 on Linux pulls CUDA 13.0.3. Torch 2.10.0 on PyPI pulls CUDA 12.8.
- Driver floors: CUDA 12.8 needs Linux 570.26 / Windows 570.65 or later. CUDA 13.x needs R580 or later under minor-version compatibility; 13.2 maps to R595.
- So 'cu126 vs cu128' is now version-bound: Blackwell needs cu128 (torch 2.7-2.11), cu129 (up to 2.13) or cu130/132.
- 2.14 also disables cuDNN conv engines 58 and 63 on sm120 to prevent illegal memory accesses.

**flash-attn.** The latest FA2 is v2.8.3.post1, re-released 2026-06-10.
- Prebuilt wheels are Linux-only (x86_64, plus one aarch64 cu13 wheel), built for torch 2.4-2.9, with no Windows wheels and no wheels for torch 2.10 or later.
- The README lists Ampere/Ada/Hopper and says Windows "might work" but needs more testing.
- setup.py builds sm_120 from source with CUDA 12.8 or later.
- FA4 is in weekly betas (4.0.0b34, 2026-10-07) for Hopper/Blackwell datacenter GPUs.

**Per engine:**
- **ACE-Step 1.5.** pyproject pins torch 2.7.1+cu128 on Windows, 2.10.0+cu128 on Linux x86_64 and 2.10.0+cu130 on aarch64; macOS uses torch 2.9.1 or later plus MLX. Python 3.11-3.12. ROCm and XPU scripts are official. It runs on Volta through Blackwell with driver 570 or later, and is official on Windows and Mac.
- **YuE2.** README: "Linux · Python 3.12 · NVIDIA GPU with BF16 support and 24 GB VRAM", one request at a time, 24 GB host RAM. pyproject pins torch==2.10.0 (PyPI, so CUDA 12.8 and sm_120 covered) and transformers 4.57.6. The fast extra is vllm 0.19.0 + triton 3.6.0. No flash-attn pin; the card says it uses FlashAttention, most likely through PyTorch SDPA, unverified. Windows and Mac are not supported. It needs Ampere or newer for BF16.
- **MiniMax-Music3.** "Inference requires CUDA." The card still says to install diffusers from the commit of PR #14456. That PR was merged 2026-08-13 and ships in diffusers v0.40.0 (2026-08-20) and v0.41.0 (2026-10-06), so the pin is obsolete. Fits 24GB+; about 22 GB with automatic CPU offload; 8 GB with layer streaming. Serving is via SGLang-Omni or ComfyUI. Windows is plausible through diffusers or ComfyUI but undocumented.
- **Shao.** The Dockerfile is FROM nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.02-py3: CUDA 12.8.0.38, PyTorch 2.7.0a0, Transformer Engine 2.0, Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.12, driver 570 or later. NVIDIA calls it Blackwell-optimised but lists known issues: Nvfuser lacks sm_120 and cuSPARSELt lacks Blackwell. The README (2026-06-16) says output is "verified ... on H800" and "can also work on RTX 4090", and that other stacks "may lead to severely degraded output, including noise-like audio". It needs Docker plus the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, so on Windows it would have to run under WSL2 (undocumented).

**By GPU generation:**
- Pascal or Turing: YuE2, MiniMax-BF16 and FA2 are out. ACE is limited on Pascal because its cu128 pin excludes Pascal.
- Ampere or Ada (RTX 30/40): everything has been tested, and this is the safest target.
- Blackwell (RTX 50): ACE, YuE2 and MiniMax should work with cu128 or later, unmeasured. Shao is numerically unverified.

Conclusion: per-engine pinned environments are mandatory. A pinned container for Shao is non-negotiable. YuE2 and Shao require Linux. ACE alone runs natively on all three OSes.

results.question: Training-cost claims: ACE-Step about 46K A100-hours ($55-76K); YuE $200-300K+ on a 512-GPU cluster with documented catastrophic failures; LoRA $100-300 and DPO $200-800 budgets.
results.finding:
**ACE-Step.** The 46K A100-hour figure matches ACE-Step v1 (arXiv 2506.00045), not v1.5.
- The v1 tables give 120 A100s (15 nodes x 8) for the DiT, about 264 hours (31,680 A100-h), and 120 A100s for about 5 days for the DCAE/VAE (about 14,400 A100-h). Together that is about 46,080 A100-h.
- The $55-76K range is derived, not stated. It implies $1.19-1.65 per A100-hour, which matches RunPod A100-80 Pod rates today. At Vast's median A100 rates it would be about $28-46K.
- The ACE-Step 1.5 paper (arXiv 2602.00744) gives no GPU-hours or cost. It says only that the VAE "undergoes adversarial tuning for 600k steps on 120 A100 GPUs" and that foundation pretraining used about 20 million text-to-music pairs, from a 27M-sample corpus. v1 used about 1.8M pieces, so v1.5 compute was very likely larger, but it is unstated.

**YuE.** The 512-GPU cluster is YuE1 (arXiv 2503.08638).
- The paper trains 0.5B/2B/7B models "on 32, 96, and 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs" and takes the 7B model to 1.75T tokens plus 40B of annealing.
- No dollar cost or GPU-hours are given. I estimate 6ND ≈ 7.5e22 FLOPs, which is about 55-70K H800-hours at 30-40% MFU, or about $110-210K at $2-3/hr for the 7B run alone. On that rough basis, $200-300K+ in total is plausible but unsourced.
- The paper documents named failure modes rather than training crashes. One is "catastrophic inertia": larger models failed to align to lyrics. Another: text conditioning "leads to complete failure beyond 6K tokens."
- YuE2 (arXiv 2609.33757) used only "64 H800 GPUs" for all phases: 60k AR + 40k joint + 6k annealing updates, global batch 256, 3.58B parameters. It also states no cost.

**LoRA.** The ACE-Step 1.5 README says "8 songs, 1 hour on 3090 (12GB VRAM)", which is vendor-claimed. One run costs about $0.25-0.70 at Vast or RunPod 3090-class rates.
- $100-300 is only realistic as an all-in budget for dozens of runs plus evaluation renders. It is not the cost of a single adapter.
- The YuE2 public repo has no fine-tuning or LoRA code, which is a feature gap for YuE2 adapters.

**DPO.** The ACE-Step 1.5 paper has no DPO; it describes "intrinsic reinforcement learning" with no external reward model or human preferences. No official DPO recipe was found in the ACE, YuE2 or MiniMax primary sources, so the $200-800 figure is unanchored. It is plausible as GPU spend on 1-2 rented 24-48GB GPUs, but it is not sourced.

Scratch training stays ruled out: tens of thousands of A100/H800-hours.
results.corrected_value: About 46K A100-h is ACE-Step v1 (31.7K DiT + 14.4K VAE), not v1.5; dollar figures are derived. YuE1 7B used 512 H800s for 1.79T tokens, with no cost stated; YuE2 used 64 H800s. ACE LoRA compute is about $1 or less per run (vendor: 1 h on a 3090); $100-300 makes sense only as an iteration budget. The DPO budget has no primary anchor.

results.question: Licenses and fitness of the proposed scorers: audiobox-aesthetics (code and weights), SongEval (README CC BY-NC-SA vs Apache metadata), the model behind 'MuLan-CLAP' (MuQ-MuLan or LAION-CLAP) and the ASR model for lyric-WER.
results.finding:
Only two of the four proposed scorers can ship in a commercial or shareable reranker or reward model: audiobox-aesthetics and the ASR. SongEval and MuQ-MuLan are non-commercial, so Kimi's plan to use all four as reranker and DPO reward cannot ship. GPT's SongEval license-conflict claim is confirmed.

(1) audiobox-aesthetics: the repo LICENSE is CC-BY-4.0. The README says most of it is CC-BY 4.0, with the bundled unilm code under MIT. The HF card facebook/audiobox-aesthetics is cc-by-4.0 and not gated. Commercial use is allowed with attribution.
- Fitness: infer.py resamples to 16 kHz in 10 s windows, so it cannot see content above 8 kHz.
- In WildSongBench every frontier system lands in a narrow PQ band (7.87 to 8.40), and LeVo 2 tops PQ (8.40) despite ranking 9th overall.
- The DiffRhythm+ authors write that Audiobox scores 'may not always align with human ratings' and that several models exceed ground truth on it.

(2) SongEval: the source files conflict.
- The GitHub LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 (initial commit 2025-05-14, never changed), and GitHub reports Apache-2.0.
- The README badge and License section say CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and 'non-commercial purposes'.
- The HF dataset ASLP-lab/SongEval is cc-by-nc-sa-4.0.
- Decisively, eval.py loads OpenMuQ/MuQ-large-msd-iter, whose weights are CC-BY-NC-4.0. Treat SongEval as non-commercial.

(3) 'MuLan' as used in WildSongBench and YuE2 is MuQ-MuLan.
- MuQ code is MIT. The MuQ-MuLan-large and MuQ-large-msd-iter weights are CC-BY-NC 4.0 (README and HF cards).
- MuQ 'strictly require[s] 24 kHz' input.
- The permissive alternative is LAION-CLAP: the repo is CC0-1.0, the lukewys/laion_clap checkpoints (including the music checkpoints) are cc0-1.0, and the HF transformers ports (laion/larger_clap_music etc.) are apache-2.0.

(4) ASR for lyric WER/PER, all permissive:
- Whisper: code MIT; large-v3 weights apache-2.0; large-v3-turbo weights mit.
- Qwen3-ASR 0.6B/1.7B: code and weights Apache-2.0. This is the ASR WildSongBench uses for PER.
- HeartTranscriptor-oss: Apache-2.0, a Whisper fine-tuned on sung lyrics.
- The HeartMuLa paper states that mainstream ASR like Whisper struggles on singing.
- WildSongBench takes the lowest PER of 4 ASR passes per candidate, which signals that ASR on singing is noisy.

Also non-commercial: Tencent SongBench (LICENSE.txt is academic-only, 'refrain from using it for any commercial or production purposes', even though its README badge says MIT; it also loads MuQ).

Fitness overall: none of these scorers inspects content above 8 to 12 kHz. Automatic scores mis-ranked Suno v6 against expert listeners (see qe-2), so treat them as diagnostics, not targets.

results.question: Does WildSongBench exist? What is its method and current scores (ACE-Step 6.01, Suno v5 6.87, YuE2 6.73/6.96, Suno v6 below v5)? Which Music Arena leaderboard gives v5 1293 and v6 1142 Elo, and are those scales comparable?
results.finding:
WildSongBench exists. It is m-a-p/WildSongBench on HF (no license tag), released with YuE2 (arXiv 2609.33757, submitted 2026-09-27), with results updated 2026-09-12.

Method:
- 192 prompts (94 zh / 98 en) with style and lyrics; no audio is included.
- All scoring is automatic. The metrics are SongBench (Tencent, 7 dimensions, MuQ-based, academic-only license), SongEval, AudioBox PQ, MuQ-MuLan, AllMusicCaps, Q3O (Qwen3-Omni prompt adherence) and PER via Qwen3-ASR.
- Candidate selection differs by system. The standard protocol takes the lower-PER of 2 candidates (4 ASR passes each). YuE2 best-of-8 selects by SongBench Musicality, then Q3O, then PER, so it is selected on the headline metric itself. Earlier proprietary systems 'retain their delivered-candidate protocols'.
- The authors state 'not a matched-compute comparison' and say the small gaps are not claims of significance.

Scores confirmed (SongBench Avg): ACE-Step 1.5 6.0118, Suno v5 6.8721, YuE2 6.7316, YuE2 Bo8 6.9632, Suno v6 6.5562, Suno v6 Wild 6.4195. Suno v6 is below v5 on SongBench and on SongEval (4.3086 vs 4.3579).

The paper's own expert listening contradicts the automatic ranking (Table 21, tie-adjusted, CR1 CIs). GPT's 'v6 strongly preferred' claim is confirmed.
- Overall, YuE2 Bo8 vs Suno v5 is 50.2% (44.0 to 56.5): balanced.
- YuE2 Bo8 vs Suno v6 is 36.1% (28.0 to 44.2, p=0.0012). As raw shares, 59.3% favor v6 vs 31.6%, 'despite YuE2 (best-of-8)'s higher SongBench Avg.'

- 1142 is Suno v6 on Artificial Analysis AA-Music-Vocal v1.1 (1142 ±15, n=2,077). Instrumental v1.1 has v6 at 1140.
- The v1.1 boards are panel-only ('Public votes cast in the Music Arena do not enter the rating calculation'), fit with Bradley-Terry MLE rescaled to an Elo-like range, and anchor MiniMax Music 3.0 at 1000.
- Suno v5 is not listed on either v1.1 board.

The scales are not comparable: different rating pools, anchors, prompt sets and organisations. A secondary report of AA's own note says cross-version comparisons 'have limited meaning'. results.question: Is there primary evidence that best-of-n reranking closes 1/3 to 1/2 of the perceptual gap to Suno, and evidence that Suno internally generates and ranks hidden candidates?
results.finding:
No primary source supports the '1/3 to 1/2 of the perceptual gap' figure. The closest primary human evidence points the other way.

YuE2 expert listening (arXiv 2609.33757, Tables 21/22), comparing 2-candidate PER-selected YuE2 against best-of-8 YuE2, both vs the same proprietary baselines:
- Average overall preference across six proprietary systems: 48.0% to 48.4% (CIs 43.8 to 52.2 and 44.8 to 52.0), essentially no change.
- vs Suno v5: 45.8% to 50.2%.
- vs Suno v6: 40.0% to 36.1% (worse).
- vs v5.5: 47.1% to 44.2%. vs v6 Wild: 51.2% to 47.5%.
- vs v4.5: 55.6% to 63.4% (the only clear gain).
- Audio-quality preference rose only modestly (56.6% to 58.9% average).
- Meanwhile the selection metric itself rose from 6.73 to 6.96 on SongBench. The automatic gain largely did not transfer to listeners.
- Caveat: these are separate pairwise studies, not a within-subject ablation.

CMI-RewardBench (arXiv 2603.00610, ICML 2026) ran best-of-N with N in {1, 3, 10} on MusicGen-small and Stable-Audio-Open-small with human A/B. It found:
- 'Ground Truth (GT) is consistently preferred over all reranked outputs'.
- Preferences 'are not strictly monotonic with N'.
- Gains 'can saturate', with 'diminishing returns beyond moderate N'.

TuneJury (arXiv 2606.17006) reports best-of-N gains on its own reward axis. Both reward models are CC-BY-NC.

Suno internals:
- Suno's v6 FAQ says only 'Each time you generate, you make two songs with a total cost of 10 credits'.
- Max Mode lets v6 'spend more on getting it right', with no mechanism disclosed.
- The 'Introducing v6' post (2026-09-09) says nothing about candidate generation or ranking.
- No primary source establishes hidden candidate generation or ranking, or '2 to 4 survivors' (the documented count is 2).

Claude Fable's point that 2 versions is the cheapest lever is consistent with practice: WSB's 2-candidate budget 'mirrors proprietary interfaces that return two songs per request'. But best-of-n should be judged by blind human A/B, not by the selector's own metric.
results.corrected_value: No support for 1/3 to 1/2. YuE2 human evidence: best-of-8 moved average overall preference vs six proprietary systems from 48.0% to 48.4% and vs Suno v6 from 40.0% to 36.1%. Suno documents 2 songs per generation; internal candidate ranking is undisclosed.

results.question: Mastering and enhancement tool licenses and claims: Matchering 2.0 (GPL?), pyloudnorm (MIT?), AudioSR and Apollo code and weight licenses, whether super-resolution adds real detail or artifacts on music, and the BS.1770-5 measurement requirements.
results.finding:
Matchering:
- GPL-3.0 (repo LICENSE; PyPI 'GPLv3'). The latest release is 2.0.6 (2022-10-19), though the repo was pushed 2026-10-07.
- It matches RMS, frequency response, peak amplitude and stereo width to a user-supplied REFERENCE track, with its own Hyrax brickwall limiter. It does not target LUFS.
- GPL matters if AURA is distributed and links it in-process. Running it as a separate process or container limits that coupling.

pyloudnorm:
- MIT, v0.2.0. It implements BS.1770-4 (README) plus EBU Tech 3342 LRA.
- It has no true-peak meter. normalize.peak() uses np.max(abs(x)), i.e. sample peak, and normalize.loudness() is a static gain that only warns on possible clipping. Kimi's '-14 LUFS / -1 dBTP with pyloudnorm' is therefore incomplete: dBTP needs an oversampled true-peak meter and a limiter.

AudioSR:
- Code MIT. The default weights haoheliu/audiosr_basic are apache-2.0. audiosr_speech has no license tag.
- It is a 'diffusion-based generative model' producing '24kHz bandwidth with a sampling rate of 48kHz' (arXiv 2309.07314). Content above the cutoff is synthesized, not recovered.
- Its README says it was 'not trained to handle other causes of high-frequency loss, such as MP3 compression', fails on unfamiliar cutoff patterns, and recommends low-pass filtering first.

Apollo:
- Code and weights are CC BY-SA 4.0 (LICENSE, README, HF JusperLee/Apollo cc-by-sa-4.0), not MIT.
- It is a GAN restoration model for lossy-MP3 music, evaluated at 44.1 kHz. It is not a 48 kHz upsampler.

GPT's 'upsampling changes the container, not the information' is supported for any real information content. Generative SR may add plausible detail or artifacts, and the proposed automatic scorers cannot even see above 8 to 12 kHz (see qe-1).

ITU-R BS.1770-5 (11/2023) is the in-force version (BS.1770-4 superseded; no -6 listed). Annex 1:
- K-weighting, with filter coefficients specified at 48 kHz.
- 400 ms gating blocks with 75% overlap.
- An absolute gate at -70 LKFS and a relative gate at -10 dB.

Annex 2 (true peak): attenuate 12.04 dB, then at least 4x oversampling (48 to 192 kHz), low-pass, absolute value, dB TP. Higher oversampling is preferred. -5 adds Annexes 3/4 for advanced sound systems and object-based audio.

BS.1770 defines measurement only, not targets. Targets are destination-dependent. For example, AA's Music Arena normalizes to -16 LUFS with a -1 dBTP ceiling and re-encodes to 320 kbps MP3 at 44.1 kHz.

results.question: Native output codec, sample rate and channel format per candidate engine (ACE-Step 48kHz VAE; MiniMax 32kHz/16-bit stereo Flow-VAE; YuE2 48kHz stereo VAE; HeartCodec; Stable Audio 3 44.1kHz), and whether each codec can be run standalone for a round-trip ceiling study.
results.finding:
GPT's extracted values are confirmed.

ACE-Step 1.5:
- VAE config: diffusers AutoencoderOobleck, sampling_rate 48000, audio_channels 2, latent dim 64, downsampling 1920x (25 Hz latents).
- A standalone VAE (ACE-Step/ace-step-v1.5-1d-vae-stable-audio-format, MIT) supports round-trip.

MiniMax Music 3:
- README: 'produces 32 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV audio'.
- Pipeline: 8-layer RVQ tokens (semantic codebook 16,384 + 7 x 1,024) feed an 8B Global + 0.6B Local LLM. Fused hidden states go to Flow Matching (2.4B), then Flow-VAE latent, then the Flow-VAE decoder (123M), giving 32 kHz stereo.
- 'waveform synthesis uses the fused LLM hidden states and does not require the discrete tokenizer decoder'. The repo ships flowmatching_vae.pth and dav.pth but documents no standalone encode-decode path. Round-trip is undocumented.

YuE2:
- YuE2-Vae 'turns acoustic latents into 48 kHz stereo music'. Latents are [T, 64], output length 1920*T-64 (25 Hz).
- Encode and decode are both documented standalone. Benchmarks use YuE2-Vae-legacy and listening uses YuE2-Vae.

HeartCodec:
- 12.5 Hz, residual VQ with K=8 codebooks of 8192, and a ~1.5B flow-matching decoder onto a 25 Hz SQ-Codec latent. Input and reconstruction are 48 kHz stereo.
- HeartCodec-oss-encoder (Apache-2.0) plus HeartCodec-oss-20260123 enable round-trip ('converts mono or stereo audio into discrete tokens and reconstructs 48 kHz stereo audio').

Stable Audio 3: SAME autoencoder, 'stereo, 44.1 kHz, 256-dimensional latents'. AutoencoderModel.from_pretrained('same-l') encode and decode are documented.

Kimi's claim that '2026 SOTA moved from RVQ to FSQ/CVQ' is refuted for these engines:
- MiniMax Music 3 and HeartCodec both use RVQ.
- ACE-Step, YuE2 and SA3 use continuous VAEs.
- The real shared trend is low frame rate (12.5 to 25 Hz) plus continuous or flow-matching decoding.

results.question: Do the cited DPO recipes for music (DiffRhythm+, Tango2) exist, what do they report, and do they address reward hacking and diversity collapse?
results.finding:
Both recipes exist. Neither measures reward hacking or diversity collapse, and both build preference pairs with the same kind of automatic scorer that is then used to report gains.

Tango 2 (arXiv 2404.09956, ACM MM 2024):
- General text-to-audio (AudioCaps-style), not music. It fine-tunes Tango with diffusion-DPO.
- Pairs are synthetic (the Audio-alpaca set): LLM prompt perturbation plus CLAP-score re-ranking, filtered by thresholds from two LAION-CLAP checkpoints.
- It reports gains in objective and human evaluation. The only safeguard is the standard DPO beta-KL term to stay near the SFT reference, plus CLAP-gap thresholds. It does not discuss reward hacking or diversity.
- Tango2 weights are cc-by-nc-sa-4.0; Audio-alpaca is apache-2.0.

DiffRhythm+ (arXiv 2507.12890):
- Full-song diffusion-DPO 'inspired by Tango2'.
- Win/lose pairs are scored by SongEval (Audiobox for instrumentals): gap of at least 0.4, winner above 3/5, beta=2000, LR 1e-6, 8 epochs on 8 GPUs (GPU type not stated).
- It reports DPO as the best stage in its ablation (score 3.19 vs SFT 2.86). Generated winners beat ground-truth winners. Too many epochs or too large a gap hurt: the authors say 'overly aggressive settings risk instability or overfitting'.
- Its reported content-quality metrics are the same SongEval and Audiobox used to build the pairs, so the evaluation is circular. It also used them to filter SFT data.
- It notes Audiobox 'discrepancies with human evaluations' and models exceeding ground truth on Audiobox.
- It reports no diversity metric.

Evaluator reuse is documented by the YuE2 / WildSongBench authors. HeartMuLa used SongEval to filter SFT data and SongEval + AudioBox to build its DPO set. It then tops SongEval Avg (4.5519, above every proprietary system) while ranking last of 17 on Q3O prompt control (3.49) and 12th on SongBench (6.25).

Kimi's '$200 to 800' cost and 'KL guard' framing: the KL term is intrinsic to DPO. The cost figure has no primary source and is unverifiable.
results.corrected_value: Tango2 = text-to-audio (not music), CLAP-ranked synthetic pairs, NC-SA weights. DiffRhythm+ = song DPO with SongEval/Audiobox pairs, beta=2000, evaluated on the same scorers. Neither measures reward hacking or diversity. HeartMuLa shows inflated SongEval vs weak prompt control after scorer-based DPO.

results.question: Training-data doctrine sources: what licenses actually apply to MTG-Jamendo tracks (any noncommercial or ND?) and FMA tracks? Is the 'CC cores' subset clean for commercial or shareable adapters?
results.finding:
Kimi's 'CC0/CC-BY doctrine' does not describe these datasets. Both are dominated by NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks.

MTG-Jamendo, by my tally of the primary per-track file audio_licenses.txt (55,701 tracks):

| License | Tracks |
|---|---:|
| CC BY-NC-SA | 21,399 |
| CC BY-NC-ND | 15,584 |
| CC BY-SA | 9,933 |
| CC BY-ND | 3,303 |
| CC BY | 3,122 |
| CC BY-NC | 2,274 |

- About 70% are NonCommercial, about 34% are NoDerivatives, and there are 0 CC0 tracks.
- The repo metadata is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the code is Apache-2.0.
- A notice added 2025-07-02 'that Jamendo requested' says the dataset 'is made available solely for non-commercial research and academic use. Any other use... requires prior written authorization from Jamendo S.A.'

FMA:
- README: 'We do not hold the copyright on the audio and distribute it under the license chosen by the artist' and 'The dataset is meant for research purposes'.
- The paper says only redistribution-permitting tracks were kept (2,616 excluded), which still admits NC and ND licenses. Code is MIT and metadata CC BY 4.0.
- A third-party HF tabulation of FMA's per-track license field (secondary, benjamin-paine/free-music-archive-full) puts about 90% of duration under NC variants, about 6% under CC-BY of any version and 0.13% under CC0. Its commercial-only pack holds 8,802 of 106,574 tracks.

The 'CC cores' are not clean for a commercial or shareable adapter:
- The CC-BY + CC-BY-SA subsets do exist (MTG-Jamendo 3,122 + 9,933 tracks).
- Jamendo's dataset-level non-commercial notice conflicts with the per-track CC-BY grants. This is contested and not resolvable from the sources.
- BY-SA ShareAlike obligations on 'Adapted Material' could reach a LoRA, which is a legal question.
- Attribution would need to be carried per track.

GPT's point stands: obtaining audio is not a training permission. Record per-track license and source for every clip, and exclude NC/ND outright for anything shareable.

new_discoveries: YuE2 open weights (YuE2-3B, YuE2-Vae, YuE2-Vae-legacy) are CC-BY-NC-4.0, a regression from YuE1's Apache-2.0. The official runtime is Linux plus a 24 GB NVIDIA GPU, so YuE2 cannot be a shippable engine and cannot run natively on the M5 Pro.

The YuE2 paper's expert listening shows automatic scorers mis-rank the frontier. Suno v6 sits below v5 on SongBench and SongEval, yet experts prefer v6 over YuE2 best-of-8 (36.1% tie-adjusted for YuE2, p=0.0012) and rate best-of-8 vs v5 as balanced (50.2%). Any 'v5 parity' target defined by SongBench, SongEval, AudioBox or MuLan is unreliable. AURA needs a blind, loudness-matched human A/B harness as its acceptance gate.

Best-of-8 selected on SongBench raised SongBench from 6.73 to 6.96. The average expert overall preference vs six proprietary systems barely moved (48.0% to 48.4%), and preference vs Suno v6 fell (40.0% to 36.1%). Reranking on these scorers is not the 'highest-leverage move' the plan assumes.

Every currently available music-quality reward model or scorer except audiobox-aesthetics is non-commercial: SongEval, the MuQ / MuQ-MuLan weights, Tencent SongBench (academic-only), CMI-RM and TuneJury (CC-BY-NC, and TuneJury also depends on MERT-v1-330M, which is CC-BY-NC). A shippable reranker must be built from audiobox-aesthetics, LAION-CLAP (CC0 / Apache-2.0) and Whisper or Qwen3-ASR, or trained in-house on Jon's own preference labels.

audiobox-aesthetics scores at 16 kHz and MuQ-based scorers at 24 kHz, so none of the proposed scorers can detect bandwidth above 8 to 12 kHz. Super-resolution and 48 kHz 'quality' claims cannot be validated with them.

pyloudnorm has no true-peak meter: its peak normalisation is sample-peak, and loudness normalisation is static gain that only warns on possible clipping. Hitting -1 dBTP needs a BS.1770-5 Annex 2 true-peak measurement (at least 4x oversampling) plus a limiter.
Apollo is CC BY-SA 4.0 (code and weights) and restores 44.1 kHz lossy-MP3 music. It is not an MIT 48 kHz upsampler as Kimi stated.

The Artificial Analysis Music Arena relaunched as v1.1 (secondary coverage dated 2026-10-07). Ratings now come from a recruited panel only, use Bradley-Terry with MiniMax Music 3.0 anchored at 1000, loudness-normalise to -16 LUFS / -1 dBTP and re-encode to 320 kbps MP3 at 44.1 kHz. Suno v6 leads both boards (1142 vocal, 1140 instrumental). Suno v5 is not on v1.1, and older Elo numbers are not comparable.

HeartCodec now has a released encoder (Apache-2.0, 12.5 Hz RVQ, 48 kHz stereo round-trip). The ACE-Step 1.5 VAE is released standalone under MIT (48 kHz Oobleck), and the Stable Audio 3 SAME autoencoder (44.1 kHz) has documented encode and decode. A codec round-trip ceiling study is feasible on permissive weights for ACE-Step and HeartCodec. MiniMax Music 3 documents no standalone encoder.

MiniMax Music 3 open weights carry a Community License. Commercial UIs must display 'MiniMax-Music3', yearly revenue above $20M needs written authorization, and any hosted service must maintain IP-abuse safeguards. Officially it needs two CUDA GPUs and outputs 32 kHz, 16-bit audio.

Stable Audio 3 (released 2026) ships an official Stability MLX path for Apple Silicon, including MLX LoRA training, and CoreML support. Medium (1.4B) is open under the Stability Community License (free below $1M revenue, gated by click-through). It appears instrumental-only: no lyrics or vocal capability is documented.

The WildSongBench prompts on HF carry no license tag, and the evaluator needs Linux, an 80 GB GPU for Q3O and about 83 GB of evaluator weights. With about 8.5 GiB free on the Mac, local reproduction is impossible without a Linux GPU box or external storage.

In July 2025 Jamendo had MTG add a notice restricting MTG-Jamendo to non-commercial research and academic use, with commercial use requiring Jamendo authorization. This affects any 'CC-core' adapter plan.

The paper (arXiv 2309.02612, SAMI-ByteDance, SDX23 winner, 9.80 dB on MUSDB18HQ) did not release weights. ZFTurbo/Music-Source-Separation-Training (MIT) is the main hub, and its docs/pretrained_models.md links checkpoints from many authors. Their rights differ widely: (a) ZFTurbo's own GitHub-release checkpoints, e.g. a MUSDB18HQ-only 4-stem BS-RoFormer at MUSDB SDR 9.65, with no separate weights license and training data that is academic-only; (b) viperx BS/Mel-RoFormer vocals hosted in TRvlvr/model_repo, no license; (c) KimberleyJSN/melbandroformer vocals, HF tag MIT; (d) anvuew dereverb_mel_band_roformer, dereverb_bs_roformer and BS-RoFormer, GPL-3.0; (e) Sucial dereverb-echo Mel-RoFormer, CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0; (f) HiDolen Mini-BS-RoFormer-V2, CC-BY-NC-4.0; (g) SYH99999/bs_roformer_4stems_ft, tagged apache-2.0 with an empty card. Stem counts: most are 2-stem (vocals/other) or single-target (dereverb, denoise, crowd); the multi-stem ones are 4-stem; plus DrumSep models with 4–6 drum parts. The only open-architecture 6-way checkpoint is 'BS-RoFormer SW' (bass, drums, other, vocals, guitar, piano). Its uploader's HF account (jarredou) is deleted, the surviving mirrors declare 'license: unknown', and they state 'Upstream declares no license… grants no additional rights'. MVSep results: on the Multisong board (4 stems plus instrumental) the top separator is the site's own MVSep Ensemble (bass 14.85, drums 14.33, other 9.01, vocals 11.93). BS Roformer SW (6 stems) scores bass 14.62, drums 14.11, other 8.72, vocals 11.30; for scale, ZFTurbo lists htdemucs at about 8.24 on vocals. On the guitar and piano boards, BS Roformer SW is rank 1 (guitar 9.01, piano 7.80), with 'Logic Pro 11.2 Stem Splitter by Apple Inc.' a hair behind at 9.00 and 7.79. Lead/back vocals is a separate board, led by community karaoke Mel/BS-RoFormers at about 10.2–11.1 lead SDR. So kimi's 'open source peaks at a clean 6-way split with BS-RoFormer' is directionally right on quality but wrong on 'clean': guitar and piano SDRs of 8–9 still bleed. It is also wrong on rights: the top 6-way checkpoint has no license and unclear provenance. gpt-sol's position (MIT code does not license the checkpoints; use only provenance-verified ones) is confirmed.

results.question: SCNet: license of its released checkpoints. SAM Audio: license terms, gating, CUDA requirement, Apple Silicon feasibility, prompt types.
results.finding: SCNet: the code is MIT ('Copyright (c) 2024 starrytong'). The README's official checkpoints (SCNet and SCNet-large) are Google Drive links with no separate weights license, trained on MUSDB (4 stems: drums, bass, other, vocals). ZFTurbo re-hosts several SCNet checkpoints (Small through XL IHF, MUSDB18HQ-only) as release assets, again with no separate license; the best, SCNet XL IHF, reaches Multisong average 9.92. So gpt-sol's 'MIT with checkpoint rights to review' stands: the weights are unlabelled and trained on academic-only MUSDB. SAM Audio (facebookresearch/sam-audio; arXiv 2512.18099, 2025-12-19; a diffusion transformer trained with flow matching) is under the custom 'SAM License' (last updated 2025-11-19). It grants a royalty-free, non-exclusive, worldwide, non-transferable licence to use, reproduce, distribute and modify, with no non-commercial clause and no revenue cap. Conditions: redistribution must ship the Agreement; publications must acknowledge SAM; Trade Controls/ITAR and military end uses are barred; no reverse engineering 'to discover the underlying components'; a patent/IP-litigation termination clause; and Meta 'may modify this Agreement' with immediate effect. Checkpoints on HF (facebook/sam-audio-small/base/large, the -tv variants and sam-audio-judge) are gated with manual approval and license 'other'. PE-AV (facebook/pe-av-large) is Apache-2.0 and not gated. The README requires Python >=3.11 and a 'CUDA-compatible GPU (recommended)'. Prompt types: text (lowercase noun or verb phrases), visual (video frames plus masks), and span (time anchors), with optional span prediction and re-ranking (CLAP or Judge). Its own table gives sam-audio-large a subjective score of 4.49 on 'Instr(pro)'. Apple Silicon: a maintainer says the code is 'device-agnostic and should work' on MPS, but out of the box the decord, xformers and cuDNN-flag dependencies break on macOS; community patches in issues #29 and #73 get it running. Blaizzy/mlx-audio has an MLX port (mlx-community/sam-audio-large, ungated mirror, license 'other'), audio-only at first, which reports about 9–20 GB peak for a 143 s clip. Memory reports on CUDA are community figures: 28–38 GB peak with defaults; about 12–17 GB in bf16; a maintainer confirms large runs 30 s of audio on an A100 80 GB, and that the span predictor alone has 'several billion parameter[s]'.

results.question: Basic Pitch: license (Apache-2.0?), its single-instrument limitation, suitability for a hummed or sung monophonic melody, and Apple Silicon runtime options (CoreML, TF or ONNX).
results.finding: License: Apache-2.0, per the repo LICENSE and the README 'Copyright and License' section. The trained model files ship inside the package (basic_pitch/saved_models/icassp_2022: TF SavedModel, nmp.mlpackage CoreML, nmp.tflite, nmp.onnx), so they are covered by the same Apache-2.0 distribution. The npm sibling basic-pitch-ts is also Apache-2.0. Limitation, quoted from the README: 'Basic pitch is instrument-agnostic and supports polyphonic instruments… Basic pitch works best on one instrument at a time.' It outputs MIDI with pitch bends. Both kimi ('polyphonic with pitch bend') and gpt-sol ('best on one instrument, not a mixed-song extractor') are therefore correct. Hummed or sung melody: the ICASSP 2022 paper (arXiv 2203.09893) says the model 'generalizes to a wide variety of instruments (including vocals)', and the training-data loaders include iKala, a singing-voice set, alongside GuitarSet, MAESTRO, MedleyDB-Pitch and Slakh. A single hummed or sung line is therefore the 'one instrument' case it is built for. Spotify publishes no hum-specific benchmark, though, so hum-to-MIDI quality should be judged on Jon's own recordings, not assumed. Maintenance: the last PyPI release is 0.4.0 (2024-08-16). The README lists Python 3.7–3.11 and says 'For Mac M1 hardware, we currently only support python version 3.10'. Issue #194 (Python 3.12 / TF 2.16+ support, 2026-06) is still open.

results.question: Lyric alignment tools: WhisperX license and the licenses of its alignment models, its word accuracy on sung vocals (the +/-50ms claim), SOFA code and checkpoint terms, MFA, and SongPrep's academic-only license.
results.finding: WhisperX (m-bain/whisperX, active, pushed 2026-09-26) is BSD-2-Clause. Alignment models come from whisperx/alignment.py. English defaults to torchaudio WAV2VEC2_ASR_BASE_960H, which torchaudio says is 'Originally published by the authors of wav2vec 2.0 under MIT License'. French, German, Spanish and Italian default to VOXPOPULI_ASR_BASE_10K_*, 'published… under CC BY-NC 4.0', which is non-commercial. Most other languages use jonatasgrosman wav2vec2-xlsr-53 models (Apache-2.0). ASR via faster-whisper weights (e.g. Systran/faster-whisper-large-v3) is MIT. Diarization uses pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1 (CC-BY-4.0, HF gated with automatic approval). The '+/-50 ms on sung vocals' claim is REFUTED as unsourced. The WhisperX paper (arXiv 2303.00747) evaluates word segmentation only on speech corpora (AMI, Switchboard) with a 200 ms collar (AMI precision 84.1 / recall 60.3), and has no singing or music evaluation. The README's limitations list words that can't be aligned (numbers, symbols) and says a language-specific wav2vec2 model is needed. SOFA (qiuqiao/SOFA, 'Singing-Oriented Forced Aligner') is MIT code and claims to outperform MFA on singing. Its official release checkpoints are Mandarin and 'multilingual' singing models (about 1.1 GB zips) trained on opencpop, m4singer, opensinger and CODEY plus community data. M4Singer's dataset license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and the checkpoints have no stated license. The one English checkpoint is community-made: tgm_en_v100 in spicytigermeat/SOFA-Models, which has no repo license. Its author's discussion post states 'Public Use: Approved' and 'Commercial Use: Approved', trained on his own labelled or hand-verified data with an Arpabet phoneme set. SOFA needs lyrics given in its dictionary's phonemes, so it runs after ASR or human lyrics. MFA (Montreal-Forced-Aligner) is MIT code, actively released (v3.4.3, 2026-10-08). Its pretrained models are CC BY 4.0; the English MFA v3.1.0 model is trained only on speech corpora (Common Voice, LibriSpeech, etc.), so singing is out of domain. SongPrep is CONFIRMED academic-only. Its LICENSE says 'You agree to use the SongPrep only for academic purposes, and refrain from using it for any commercial or production purposes under any circumstances', which covers code and weights, and the weights are fine-tuned from Qwen2-7B (Apache-2.0).

results.question: all-in-one music structure analyzer: code and weight license (MIT?), the section labels it produces, Apple Silicon support. msaf as an alternative.
results.finding: all-in-one (mir-aidj/all-in-one, PyPI 'allin1') is MIT code. Its weights are on HF at taejunkim/allinone, tagged MIT and trained on the Harmonix Set: harmonix-all is an 8-fold ensemble, with harmonix-fold0 through fold7 also available. It predicts BPM, beats, downbeats, functional boundaries and labels. The 10 label classes (allin1.HARMONIX_LABELS) are start, end, intro, outro, break, bridge, inst, solo, verse and chorus; there is no pre-chorus or hook class. Internally it source-separates first with Demucs (htdemucs) and depends on 'demucs' and 'natten'. Maintenance is stale: the last PyPI release is 1.1.0 (2023-10-10) and the last repo push 2024-05-09. Several open issues and PRs report breakage with newer NATTEN (#30 for v0.17.5, #27; #37 targets NATTEN 0.21 plus torch 2.7 cu128). Apple Silicon: the README says NATTEN 'auto-installs' on macOS and the default device is 'cuda if available else cpu', so there is no MPS path. NATTEN has CUDA kernels and only a naive CPU kernel, and installs on Mac often fail (#11, #28). Open PR #39 (2026-09-20) adds a pure-PyTorch neighborhood-attention path for CPU/MPS that makes NATTEN optional, but it is unmerged. msaf (urinieto/msaf) is MIT, with the last PyPI release 0.1.80 (2023-06-25) and a repo push in 2026-05. It provides unsupervised boundary algorithms (foote, sf, olda, cnmf, scluster, vmo, cbm) and label algorithms (fmc2d, cnmf, scluster, vmo). Its labels are segment-similarity IDs ('-1' when no label algorithm is used), not functional verse/chorus names. That makes it a weaker fit for a 'Song Editor' with named sections unless an LLM or heuristic maps clusters to names.

results.weights_license: all-in-one: MIT tag on HF taejunkim/allinone (Harmonix Set annotations; the audio is not redistributed). msaf: no learned weights needed for most algorithms.

results.question: What does Suno's 2026-06-11 stem update say about how stems are produced (regenerated vs extracted), the maximum stem count (12?), the instrument-type count (about 100), and known limitations?
results.finding: The Suno blog post 'We've made improvements to Stem Separation' (Jun 11, 2026) says: 'Instead of cutting your song apart, Suno listens to it and regenerates each stem from scratch using our latest model', and 'You're getting a freshly generated guitar that matches what was there'. It describes three modes: Auto Split 'breaking a track into up to 12 stems' (drums, bass, guitar, keys, woodwinds and more), called 'reliable but less precise than the updated options' (Pro and Premier); Split from Mix, one chosen stem plus a complement track (Pro and Premier); and Advanced Split, 'a list of nearly 100 instruments' (Premier only), with 'A few of the most granular options… still in development'. The release notes (suno.com/release-notes/advanced-stems, Jun 11, 2026) call Auto Split 'Our classic model, splitting songs into 12 stem categories'. So the regeneration language belongs to the new approach, and Suno's own pages do not say outright whether the classic Auto Split also regenerates. The help articles (13925185, 12702337) use 'extraction' wording for billing. Auto Split costs 50 credits per extraction (12 stems); Split from Mix and Advanced cost 10 credits per stem. They also list limitations: Auto Split 'doesn't always label them correctly', and requesting an instrument absent from the song 'may still use credits, but it may not produce a usable stem'. Stems work on Suno songs and on 'your own music you upload', and in Suno Studio (right-click a clip, then Split Stems). Verdict on the competing claims: gpt-sol-core and gpt-sol-voice-video are confirmed (regenerated, up to 12, about 100). kimi-k3's '8 stems' is refuted, and its 'phantom reverb' and '~2% replacement success' appear in no primary source (unverifiable). claude-fable's '8 detected stems; modeled as Demucs separation' is refuted, since Suno explicitly contrasts its method with frequency-slicing separators. For AURA, Suno-class stems are a generation (re-synthesis) problem, not only a separation problem.

new_discoveries: Demucs is not frozen. The author's fork adefossez/demucs is now the official maintained Demucs and shipped v4.1.0 to PyPI on 2026-07-11. Changes: pyproject/uv; Python >=3.10; torchaudio removed from inference; safetensors weights on the HF hub (adefossez/HTDemucs, HTDemucs-ft, HTDemucs-6s); automatic MPS on Apple Silicon. Pin `demucs>=4.1.0` from adefossez, not the archived facebookresearch repo.

demucs-mlx (ssmall256, MIT, PyPI 1.6.1, 2026-10-05) now claims 114x realtime warm on a 40-core M4 Max, replacing the old '73x'. Its own table on the same machine shows stock demucs 4.1.0 on MPS at 42x. The htdemucs MLX weights are only 160 MB, which matters for the Mac's 8.5 GiB free disk. A native Swift package, demucs-mlx-swift (MIT), shares the same weights and could suit a native Mac app.

ssmall256/mlx-audio-separator (MIT) ports Roformer (BS and Mel), MDXC, MDX, VR and Demucs inference to MLX without PyTorch. This makes a Mac-local RoFormer lane realistic. mlx-community/mel-roformer-mlx (MIT tag) provides converted weights.

MVSep guitar and piano leaderboards: 'Logic Pro 11.2 Stem Splitter by Apple Inc.' is essentially tied with the best open 6-stem checkpoint (guitar 9.00 vs 9.01, piano 7.79 vs 7.80). Jon owns a Mac, and Apple's May 2025 newsroom post confirms the guitar and piano stems. For his own songs, a licensed commercial DAW gives top-tier 6-stem separation with no checkpoint-rights risk.

The best open 6-way separator, BS-RoFormer SW (bass, drums, other, vocals, guitar, piano), has no license. Its original uploader's HF account is deleted, and the surviving mirrors say they grant no rights. Keep it out of any AURA build that might be open-sourced. A GGUF build runs on Metal via BSRoformer.cpp.

Community RoFormer checkpoint licenses are all over the place: GPL-3.0 (anvuew dereverb, BS-RoFormer), CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (Sucial dereverb-echo), CC-BY-NC-4.0 (HiDolen Mini-BS-RoFormer-V2), MIT (KimberleyJSN vocals), and none (viperx/TRvlvr, ZFTurbo release assets). An allow-list per checkpoint is required.

WhisperX's default aligners for French, German, Spanish and Italian (torchaudio VoxPopuli) are CC BY-NC 4.0, i.e. non-commercial. English (wav2vec2 base 960h) is MIT. WhisperX on Mac is CPU-only (int8). Its paper evaluates only speech at a 200 ms collar, so there is no evidence for sung-lyric accuracy.

SOFA's one English singing checkpoint (tgm_en_v100, spicytigermeat/SOFA-Models) carries author-stated 'Commercial Use: Approved' in the discussion post. SOFA's own official checkpoints are Mandarin or multilingual, trained partly on M4Singer (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), with no stated license.

all-in-one is effectively unmaintained (PyPI 1.1.0 from Oct 2023) and breaks with current NATTEN. There is no MPS path; an open PR #39 from 2026-09-20 would add a pure-PyTorch CPU/MPS path. Budget for vendoring or forking it, or run it on the Linux/CUDA box.

Suno's stems also work on uploaded non-Suno audio and inside Suno Studio. Costs: Auto Split 50 credits for 12 stems, Split from Mix and Advanced 10 credits per stem; Advanced is Premier-only. Suno's help warns that labels can be wrong and that credits may be charged even when the requested instrument isn't in the song.

SAM Audio has an ungated community MLX port (mlx-community/sam-audio-large via mlx-audio). It is still subject to the SAM License (redistribution must include the Agreement), and Meta can modify that license unilaterally with immediate effect.

Basic Pitch is stale. Last PyPI release is 0.4.0 (Aug 2024), the README officially supports Python 3.10 only on Apple Silicon, and the Python 3.12 / TF 2.16 issue (#194) is open. Plan an isolated Python 3.10 environment, or use the bundled ONNX/CoreML model files directly.

results.question: What license covers the YuE2 (and legacy YuE1 7B) weights: Apache-2.0, or CC BY-NC 4.0 plus the 2026-09-16 individual-creator permission? Does that permission cover an LLC?
results.finding: gpt-sol-core is correct for YuE2. The GitHub MODEL_LICENSE (commits dated 2026-09-16) licenses the YuE2-3B, YuE2-Vae and YuE2-Vae-legacy weights under CC BY-NC 4.0. It adds an 'Individual creator permission' for 'personal users, content creators and musicians acting in an individual capacity': they may generate outputs and publish, sell, license or otherwise monetize those outputs, with no fees or royalties, subject to responsible-use conditions. The same file states the permission 'does not authorize commercial use of the model weights by companies', who must contact the licensors for a commercial license. It also states the permission 'does not extend to commercial redistribution or sale of the model weights'. An LLC such as Island Development Crew is a company, so it is NOT covered. Jon acting personally is covered. The permission text also lets individuals license their outputs 'to clients', which reads as letting Jon license a song he made personally to his LLC. That is an interpretation, not legal advice; confirm it with the licensors. Caveat: the Hugging Face LICENSE files for all three YuE2 repos are plain CC BY-NC 4.0 and do not contain the creator permission; it exists only in the GitHub MODEL_LICENSE and README. Legacy YuE1 is different: m-a-p/YuE-s1-7B-anneal-en-cot, -en-icl and YuE-s2-1B-general are still distributed on HF tagged apache-2.0, and the YuE-v1 branch README says 'The YuE model (including its weights) is now released under the Apache License, Version 2.0' (since 2025-01-30). Kimi's 'Apache-2.0' is wrong for YuE2. Claude-Fable's 'YuE 7B Apache-2.0' is right, but only for YuE1. Note that the YuE1 paper says it was trained on '650K hours of in-the-wild music recordings from the Internet', which carries a data-provenance risk despite the permissive license. For open-source AURA, Apache-2.0 code that downloads YuE2 weights at runtime is fine. Bundling or redistributing YuE2 weights in a commercial product is not allowed. Each AURA user's rights depend on their own status (individual or company).

results.question: What are YuE2's official hardware, OS and runtime requirements and generation time per 3-minute song? Is YuE1 7B still distributed, and what were its official VRAM and speed figures?
results.finding: Official YuE2 requirements: the GitHub README and docs/generation.md say 'Linux · Python 3.12 · NVIDIA GPU with BF16 support and 24 GB VRAM', 'one request at a time', 48 kHz stereo, no quantization. The HF card says 'Linux · Python 3.10+'; pyproject has requires-python >=3.10 and pins torch 2.10.0. The HF card also asks for 24 GB of available host RAM. Speed (vendor-claimed, HF card): 'A 3.6-minute song in 71 seconds on an RTX 4090' (71.04 s for 214.85 s of audio, full CoT, peak VRAM 11.18 GiB; maximum-context peak 14.08 GiB). An H800 took 54.74 s for 224.96 s. That works out to roughly 1 minute per 3-minute song on a 4090, per candidate. A separate vLLM server runtime (the 'fast' extra) does 119 to 374 songs per hour on an H800 at about 78 GiB. Mac and Windows are not official targets. The source does contain MPS branches (pipeline device='auto' falls back to mps), but open community issues report problems: #176, the pinned torch 2.10 silently corrupts BF16 causal attention on MPS (fixed in torch 2.13); #187, Metal driver memory grows until generation stalls around 8 to 9k tokens; and #209, Windows CUDA falls back to a slow attention kernel. YuE1 is still distributed: the HF YuE-s1-7B repos are live (Apache-2.0, about 12.45 GB each) and its code is preserved on the YuE-v1 branch. YuE1 official figures (YuE-v1 README): 24 GB or less runs up to 2 sessions; full songs (4+ sessions) need at least 80 GB (H800/A100 or multiple 4090s with tensor parallelism). An H800 takes 150 s per 30 s of audio and an RTX 4090 about 360 s per 30 s, which extrapolates to about 15 min and 36 min per 3-minute song. Kimi's '15 min H800 / 36 min 4090' is therefore a YuE1 figure; applying it to YuE2 is wrong. Claude-Fable's 'YuE 7B, 16GB, about 5 min' matches no official figure.
results.corrected_value: YuE2: Linux + NVIDIA BF16 24 GB (official), about 71 s per 3.6-minute song on an RTX 4090 (vendor-claimed), peak about 11 to 14 GiB VRAM, 48 kHz stereo, one request at a time. YuE1 7B: 24 GB for 2 sessions, 80 GB for full songs, about 15 min (H800) or 36 min (4090) per 3-minute song (extrapolated from official per-30 s figures).
results.hardware_notes: Official: Linux, CUDA, BF16, 24 GB VRAM, 24 GB host RAM, optional experimental FP8 for the AR stage (NVIDIA compute capability 8.9 or newer). Apple Silicon: unofficial. The code has MPS paths, but known silent-correctness and memory bugs are open (#176, #187). A community member measured 36.8 tok/s AR decode on an M5 Pro, vs the vendor's 139 tok/s on a 4090.
