results.question: What do the YuE2 paper and docs report: the human preference results against Suno v4.5/v5/v6, the WildSongBench or SongBench scores (6.73 to 6.96 with best-of-8 vs Suno v5 6.87), the best-of-8 selection method and decoder used, and the training-data hours and composition (346k hours vs 'primarily CC0 + synthetic')?
results.finding: Both sources are partly right, and the numbers reconcile. Automatic metric (WildSongBench, 192 prompts, 2026-09-12): YuE2 6.7316 and YuE2 best-of-8 6.9632 SongBench Avg, vs Suno v5 6.8721, Suno v5.5 6.7150, Suno v4.5 6.6995, Suno v6 6.5562, Suno v6 Wild 6.4195, and Mureka 9 6.9377 (the strongest proprietary system). Expert listening (arXiv 2609.33757 v1, 27 Sep 2026; YuE2 authors' own Arena; 62 paid expert annotators; 3,602 expert evaluations), overall quality for best-of-8: vs Suno v4.5, 57.3% YuE2 vs 30.5%; vs Suno v5, 40.4% vs 39.9% ('nearly balanced'); vs Suno v6, 'Suno v6 receives more overall preferences, at 59.3% versus 31.6%'. Per the figure, Suno v5.5 (47% vs 36%) and Suno v6 Wild (45% vs 40%) are also preferred over best-of-8. Audio quality is YuE2's strength: 58.9% tie-adjusted across the six proprietary baselines. docs/benchmarks.md explicitly says the automatic results 'do not establish universal metric superiority or human preference'. Selection: standard YuE2 picks the lower-PER of 2 candidates. Best-of-8 removes candidates dominated jointly in SongBench Musicality, Q3O and PER, keeps those within 0.10 of the top Musicality and then within 0.10 of the top remaining Q3O, and then picks the lowest PER, where each candidate's PER is its lowest across 4 ASR passes. The selection therefore uses an evaluator dimension. Decoder: both YuE2 benchmark settings use YuE2-Vae-legacy; default listening uses YuE2-Vae. Training data: 'approximately 346,000 hours of music', and Appendix C says 'We train MERT2, SheetSage2-AR, and YuE2 primarily on CC0 music and synthetic data. Tokenwave.AI provides most of our synthetic training data under license.' So 346k hours and 'primarily CC0 + synthetic' are both true. Kimi's '650k hours' is YuE1's corpus (650K hours of in-the-wild internet music, per the YuE1 paper), not YuE2's; MERT2 used 700,000 hours. All preference and metric results are vendor-run.
results.corrected_value: Kimi's best-of-8 claim holds only on the automatic SongBench metric. Human experts preferred Suno v6, v5.5 and v6 Wild over YuE2 best-of-8, and the v5 comparison was a tie. YuE2 training: about 346k hours, primarily CC0 plus licensed synthetic data (Tokenwave.AI). The 650k-hour figure belongs to YuE1 (in-the-wild internet music).

results.finding: wavesurfer.js core is BSD-3-Clause and very active. v8.0.0 shipped on 2026-09-23 and v8.0.2 on 2026-10-07. v8 rebuilds teardown and fixes double-firing events, and the public API is mostly unchanged. The multitrack plugin (katspaugh/wavesurfer-multitrack) is a separate repo, also BSD-3-Clause, with 44 stars. It is effectively dormant: the last npm release is 0.4.12 (2024-07-16), and the newer 0.4.13 GitHub tag (2025-02-28) never reached npm. Its README calls it 'commercial' with no free support, and the maintainer closed an out-of-sync bug report by linking that support note. It depends on wavesurfer.js ^7.6.3 and imports 'wavesurfer.js/dist/draggable.js', which the v8 release notes say is no longer built into dist/. v8 compatibility is therefore unverified and probably broken without a fork. Source review of src/multitrack.ts shows: (1) each track is one audio file with a startPosition, so there are no multiple clips per track; (2) each track has a single fadeInEnd/fadeOutStart, a volume and an optional envelope; (3) on non-iOS, every track is a separate HTMLAudioElement re-synced on requestAnimationFrame with a 0.3 s drift tolerance (precisionSeconds = 0.3), so scheduling is NOT sample-accurate; (4) there are no version lanes or takes, and no per-clip gain. Kimi's claim that it 'matches Suno Studio' is refuted. It is a waveform viewer and simple synced player, not a DAW timeline. GPT's doubt holds. Closer fits found in primary sources: naomiaro/waveform-playlist (MIT, v16.0.0, 2026-09-28; React + Tone.js) has multiple clips per track and sample-based clip positions (startSample/offsetSamples/durationSamples). It also offers per-clip gain and fadeIn/fadeOut, overlapping clips for crossfades, AudioWorklet recording and WAV export. andremichelle/openDAW is a full browser DAW but AGPL-3.0, with the SDK under AGPL-3.0-or-later. Version lanes and takes would be app-level code in any option.

results.question: Web Audio API and AudioWorklet: specification status, latency-hint behavior, and measured round-trip latency in Chrome and Safari on macOS. Can a browser Studio meet 48kHz / 256-frame buffers with 8-16 tracks?
results.finding: Spec status: Web Audio API 1.0 is a W3C Recommendation (REC-webaudio-20210617). Web Audio 1.1 is a W3C Working Draft (latest 2026-09-22), so GPT's 'draft' claim is correct for 1.1. latencyHint: the spec says a numeric hint is interpreted at the browser's discretion and the actual latency is reported by baseLatency, so there is no guarantee (GPT confirmed). MDN agrees: 'The user agent may or may not choose to meet this request'. The new renderSizeHint is 'a hint that might not be honored'. Engine behavior from source code: Chromium on macOS defaults the output hardware buffer to 256 frames at <=48 kHz (ChooseBufferSize = max(2*128, ...)). 'interactive' uses the hardware buffer size, and a numeric latencyHint maps to multiples of it (128-4096 frames). WebKit (main) parses latencyHint but ignores it ('// FIXME: Figure out where latencyHint should go.'). Whenever Web Audio is active, WebKit forces the Cocoa preferred hardware buffer to the 128-frame render quantum. AudioWorklet is Baseline (Chrome 66, Safari 14.1, Firefox 76) and requires a secure context. Measured round-trip: the only rigorous public data found is the peer-reviewed WAC 2025 MLS-loopback study (Gil Panal et al., 100 trials). On a MacBook Pro 2021 it measured Safari 100.02 ms (sd 0.00), Chrome 52.33 ms (sd 1.14) and Firefox 38.89 ms. On Windows 10 Chrome measured 62.84 ms and on Ubuntu 64.50 ms (sd 7.94). This is far above native DAW round-trip at 128-256 frames. Viability: (a) a 48 kHz output buffer of 256 frames (5.3 ms) or smaller IS met. It is Chrome's macOS default, and Safari/WKWebView runs at 128. (b) Live input monitoring/overdubbing with low round-trip is NOT met in any browser on Mac. Recording works only with latency compensation, which Hi-Audio shows can be done to within about 1 ms. (c) Whether 8-16 tracks plus effects stay glitch-free is a CPU question with no primary benchmark. It must be measured on the M5 Pro, for example with Chrome's AudioContext.playbackStats (Chrome 146+, underrun counts) or a loopback test.

results.question: Desktop shell: Tauri 2 vs Electron bundle sizes (42MB vs 168MB), and the Web Audio/AudioWorklet limitations of WKWebView inside a macOS Tauri app compared with Chromium in Electron.
results.finding: Size: the '42MB vs 168MB' figures are not bundle sizes. The only source containing them (a secondary blog, tech-insider) gives them as idle RAM. Primary: Tauri's docs say a minimal app 'can be less than 600KB' because it uses the system webview. Electron v44.7.0's own runtime archive (electron-v44.7.0-darwin-arm64.zip) is 124 MB compressed before any app code, per GitHub release metadata. Tauri is several times to orders of magnitude smaller, but 42/168 should not be cited as bundle sizes. Webview: Tauri uses WKWebView on macOS, with the WebKit version tied to the OS; WebView2 (Chromium, evergreen) on Windows; and distro-dependent webkit2gtk on Linux. Inside a macOS Tauri app, Web Audio therefore behaves like Safari. AudioWorklet works (Safari 14.1+), but WebKit ignores latencyHint (source FIXME) and pins a 128-frame buffer. WKWebView has no AudioContext sinkId/setSinkId, so the output device cannot be chosen from JS, and no renderSizeHint. outputLatency only exists from Safari 18.4. Electron 44 (Chromium 152) honors numeric latencyHint and supports setSinkId (Chrome 110+). renderSizeHint arrives in Chromium 153, so Electron 45+. GPT's VoiceStudio claim is confirmed: debpalash/VoiceStudio docs say 'Electron is the only maintained desktop app' and that Tauri was archived at v0.5.3. However, its docs give no audio-related reason for the switch, so it is not evidence that WKWebView broke audio. Important update: Tauri v3 alpha (3.0.0-alpha.4, 2026-10-01) adds a selectable 'tauri-runtime-cef' runtime (Chromium Embedded Framework, CEF 152). That would give a Tauri app Chromium audio behavior on macOS, at Electron-like size, but it is alpha. The current stable release is Tauri 2.12.2 (2026-10-09).
primary_sources: https://v2.tauri.app/start/ ('minimal Tauri app can be less than 600KB')

results.output_rights: n/a
results.hardware_notes: The Mac has only about 8.5 GiB free. An Electron toolchain plus its runtime, or Tauri-CEF, which downloads a Chromium build, will use a meaningful share of that. Neither was installed or measured. Electron 44 requires macOS 13 or later, and macOS 26.6 is fine. Bundle and RAM figures beyond the primary ones above are vendor or blog claims.

new_discoveries: wavesurfer.js 8.0.0 (2026-09-23) removed dist/draggable.js, which wavesurfer-multitrack imports. The multitrack plugin is pinned to wavesurfer ^7 and has had no npm release since 0.4.12 (2024-07). Do not build the Studio timeline on it.

naomiaro/waveform-playlist v16 (MIT, React + Tone.js) already offers multiple clips per track and sample-based clip positions. It also has per-clip gain and fades, crossfade overlaps, AudioWorklet recording and WAV export. It is the strongest permissive base for a browser timeline. openDAW is a fuller browser DAW but is AGPL-3.0.

JUCE is now at major version 9 (9.0.0 2026-07-21; 9.0.3 2026-09-28) under the JUCE 9 EULA. Its free Starter tier is capped at $20k annual revenue/funding, with no copyleft mixing allowed. Otherwise the whole app must be AGPLv3.

The Steinberg VST3 SDK is now MIT (github.com/steinbergmedia/vst3sdk). The ASIO SDK has been dual proprietary/GPLv3 since 2025-10-15. A native engine can now host VST3 plugins permissively. Enabling ASIO on Windows, for example via CPAL's 'asio' feature, brings in GPLv3 or Steinberg terms.
Signalsmith Stretch (MIT) is a permissive pitch/time-stretch alternative to Rubber Band (GPL/commercial) and SoundTouch (LGPL). It ships a WASM/AudioWorklet npm build and a Rust crate.

Tauri v3 alpha adds a selectable Chromium (CEF 152) runtime, tauri-runtime-cef. It could remove the WKWebView Web Audio gaps on macOS (no latencyHint, no setSinkId) while keeping Tauri's Rust backend, but it is alpha-only today.

WebKit ignores AudioContext latencyHint ('FIXME' in source) and has no setSinkId. A Safari or WKWebView studio cannot pick the output audio interface from JS, and Electron/Chromium can. This favors Electron, Tauri-CEF or a native audio engine with the webview as UI only.

Chrome 153 adds renderSizeHint (configurable render quantum; chromestatus desktop milestone 153), and Chrome 146 adds AudioContext.playbackStats (underrun counts per MDN browser-compat-data). Safari has neither, and both standards positions show 'No signal'. playbackStats is a ready tool to measure whether 8-16 tracks run glitch-free on the M5 Pro.

The peer-reviewed WAC 2025 study measured browser round-trip latency on a MacBook Pro 2021: Safari about 100 ms, Chrome about 52 ms, Firefox about 39 ms. Browser-based live monitoring for vocal overdubs is not viable. Plan for latency-compensated recording, or a native engine (CPAL/JUCE) for input monitoring.

results.question: Suno v6 facts: release date, variants, max length, Max Mode, Variety, multi-reference role binding, section/word edits, older-model retirement, existence of v6.5.

The help article 'What's new in v6?' says v6 and v6-wild are Pro/Premier only, v6-mini is on all plans, and 'All three variants support up to 8 minutes per generation.'

It is recommended for songs over 2 minutes, close covers, style transfer, and keeping vocals consistent. The pricing page lists a max_mode flag on Pro and Premier only. Suno's Sep 2026 Terms give Suno a 'perpetual, irrevocable', sublicensable, uncompensated license to user Submissions, including voice and likeness, to 'train, develop, fine-tune' its models. If the owner uploads his melody or voice to Suno for the paid first attempt, Suno gets a training license on it. Commercial use of Suno output also requires a 'permitted download', which ties rights to the 20/60 monthly cap.

Suno's stem separation (blog post, Jun 11, 2026) 'regenerates each stem from scratch with its latest model' rather than separating the mix. Suno stems are therefore generative re-synthesis, which matters for how AURA's 'isolation/stems' parity target should be specified. Auto Split gives up to 12 stems; Advanced Split covers about 100 instruments and is Premier-only.

Suno launched 'Speech (beta)' on Oct 1, 2026, open to everyone, which 'generates voice and music together as one cohesive track'. This bears on the Sabbath Echo narration opportunity, though plan, commercial and language terms are not stated.

Gemini API Lyria 3.5 costs $0.08 per full song (44.1 kHz stereo, SynthID-watermarked, single-turn with no editing). It is the cheapest hosted benchmark or reference lane. The Artificial Analysis v1.1 boards put Mureka V9.5 (#3 vocal, 1103) above Lyria 3.5 and ElevenLabs, which makes Mureka's pinnable mureka-9.5 API (stems with MIDI, region edit) the strongest hosted fallback.

In the YuE2 WildSongBench table, ACE-Step 1.5 scores SongBench Avg 6.01 against Suno v6 at 6.56, YuE2 best-of-8 at 6.96 and Mureka 9 at 6.94. This is vendor-paper evidence that an ACE-Step-only design would fall well short of v6-class, which supports the owner's 'not ACE-Step-only' instruction.

GEMA v. Suno (LG München I, Jul 31, 2026, not final) held memorization in model weights to be reproduction and the provider liable for outputs. It also rejected the TDM exception and US fair use. This is a data-provenance risk for any AURA fine-tune on scraped commercial music if the model or outputs are distributed in the EU.

The bundled pymss/pymss_core separation backend (it replaced UVR5 on 2026-07-22) and the new RVCRealtimeVST plugin are also MIT. All pretrained assets come from one HF repo, lj1995/VoiceConversionWebUI: hubert_base, rmvpe.pt/.onnx, pretrained/ and pretrained_v2/ G/D 32k/40k/48k, and mute.zip. That repo is ungated and tagged `license: mit` in its metadata only; it holds no license text. Upstream of those assets: ContentVec (credited by RVC) is MIT and fairseq HuBERT is MIT. RMVPE's paper code (Dream-High/RMVPE) is Apache-2.0. The yxlllc/RMVPE fork, whose weights RVC says were trained by yxlllc and RVC-Boss, has no LICENSE on GitHub, so the rmvpe.pt weights carry only lj1995's MIT tag. results.question: OpenVPI DiffSinger: code license, availability and terms of high-quality voicebanks and vocoders, Apple Silicon inference support, and the effort needed to make a bank from Jon's voice.
results.finding: The code is Apache-2.0 (openvpi/DiffSinger, latest release v2.5.1 on 2026-01-08, still active with commits in September 2026). The README disclaimer forbids generating anyone's voice without their consent. The community vocoder is a trap: the universal pre-trained NSF-HiFiGAN (2022-12 v1, the 2024-02 44.1k/hop512/128-bin release, and PC-NSF-HiFiGAN 2025-02) carries weights 'licensed under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0', with attribution required on redistribution. That is non-commercial and share-alike, so a commercial song needs a self-trained vocoder. The vocoder training code, openvpi/SingingVocoders, is MIT. The openvpi/vocoders site repo is AGPL-3.0. Voicebanks are distributed by individual community creators, mostly for OpenUtau, each under its own terms; OpenVPI publishes no general voicebank license. Tools: MakeDiffSinger is BSD-3-Clause, dataset-tools Apache-2.0, SOME (MIDI extraction) MIT, OpenUtau MIT. Apple Silicon: DiffSinger's PyTorch inference, binarizer and exporter choose 'cuda' when available and otherwise 'cpu' (base_svs_infer.py, binarizer_utils.py, export.py), so Python inference on a Mac runs on CPU. Training uses pl_trainer_accelerator 'auto', and utils/training_utils.py imports Lightning's MPSAccelerator, but MPS training is not documented and the default precision is '16-mixed'. Production inference goes through ONNX export into OpenUtau, which ships an osx-arm64 .dmg (release 0.1.574.1-alpha, 2026-10-09) and offers a CoreML ONNX runner on macOS. Effort to build a bank from Jon's voice: record clean, unaccompanied single-singer WAVs above 32 kHz. Slice them into 5-15 s segments with AudioSlicer, then label the lyric syllables of every segment against a dictionary with MinLabel. Run Montreal Forced Aligner (conda, MFA 2.0.6); MakeDiffSinger documents an MFA model only for the 'Opencpop extension' (Mandarin) dictionary, so English needs a community dictionary and MFA model. Every phoneme needs coverage, with at least 20 occurrences recommended. Then build the variance dataset (MIDI/DS editing with SlurCutter or SOME), train the acoustic and variance models, and ideally fine-tune a vocoder. The docs state no data-hour minimum. Score preparation (notes plus lyrics) is required at inference.

results.question: pyannote speaker verification: code license and the gating and terms of its embedding models, plus suitability for a read-aloud consent check. What exactly does Suno's voice flow require (minimum length, phrase check)?
results.finding: pyannote.audio is MIT and is primarily a diarization toolkit; the open pipeline is community-1, and the premium precision-2 runs on pyannoteAI servers with an API key. Embedding models: pyannote/embedding is MIT but gated ('auto'), requiring an HF token plus a form (company/university, website, intended use), and its prompt asks companies to consider contributing back. pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM is CC-BY-4.0 and ungated (attribution required), wraps WeSpeaker, and its card shows exactly the cosine-distance speaker-verification recipe; it needs pyannote.audio >= 3.1. pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1 is CC-BY-4.0 and gated, and accepting it consents to occasional marketing email. An ungated alternative is speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb (Apache-2.0). Suitability: pyannote can automate only the 'same speaker?' half of a consent gate (voiceprint similarity between the read phrase and the singing sample). It cannot check that the displayed phrase was actually spoken; that needs an ASR step such as Whisper or Qwen3-ASR plus a text match. Speaker-match thresholds between speech and singing are not documented by pyannote and would need calibration. So 'pyannote automates Suno's phrase gate' is only half right, and a checkbox alone is weaker than Suno's actual flow. Suno's flow per the official help article: source audio 'from 15 seconds up to 4 minutes', you 'choose the best 2 minutes', a cappella recommended (Suno isolates vocals otherwise). Suno 'will display a short phrase for you to read aloud'; it is spoken, not sung. That recording is 'compared against your uploaded singing recording to confirm they are from the same person', and the system also checks that you said the displayed words. You must 'Check the confirmation box to affirm that you have the rights to use this voice'. Voices is 18+ only and may be region-limited. The Suno product page instead says 'Record at least ten seconds of your voice' and that a recorded or uploaded Voice is private; that conflicts with the help article's 15 s minimum. The pricing page lists 'Record, upload, and create with your own voice' on Pro ($8/mo) and Premier ($24/mo), not Free.
results.corrected_value: Consent gate = speaker embedding match (pyannote WeSpeaker CC-BY-4.0 ungated, or SpeechBrain ECAPA Apache-2.0) + ASR phrase match + rights checkbox + consent_at. Suno minimum: 15 s per the help article (10 s per the product page), max 4 min, 2-min selection, spoken phrase, rights checkbox, 18+.

results.weights_license: pyannote/embedding MIT, gated (form + HF token). pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM CC-BY-4.0, ungated. speaker-diarization-community-1 CC-BY-4.0, gated (marketing-email consent). speaker-diarization-3.1 MIT, gated. speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb Apache-2.0, ungated.

new_discoveries: Seed-VC (Plachtaa/seed-vc) is now ARCHIVED and read-only, with its last commit on 2025-04-20. Its code and its HF weights are both GPL-3.0. It should not be a core dependency of AURA; treat it as an optional, separate-process audition tool at most.

Upstream RVC dropped Apple Silicon. Release 2.3.260718 (July 2026) picks CUDA, then DirectML, then CPU, and the README covers only Ubuntu 24.04 and Windows. The old 2.2.231006 tag had MPS. On the M5 Pro, use the community fork Applio (MIT, MPS training) or run RVC on the Linux/Windows NVIDIA box. RVC also replaced UVR5 with PyMSS (MIT; it includes BS-RoFormer and MLX variants) and added a realtime VST2/VST3 plugin that is Windows-only and needs CUDA.

The DiffSinger community NSF-HiFiGAN and PC-NSF-HiFiGAN vocoder weights are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so a commercial song from a DiffSinger bank needs a vocoder trained with openvpi/SingingVocoders (MIT). On Mac, run DiffSinger through OpenUtau (MIT, osx-arm64 build, CoreML ONNX runner), because DiffSinger's own Python inference has no MPS path.

VoiceStudio's default engine, OmniVoice, has CC-BY-NC weights, and its audio tokenizer carries Higgs Audio 2 and Llama terms. A VoiceStudio Pro or commercial license does not cure this, so VoiceStudio-as-shipped is not a commercial Sabbath Echo narration path. Its ~10 GB macOS disk requirement also exceeds Jon's ~8.5 GiB free.

Chatterbox added Multilingual V3 (0.5B) and Chatterbox-Nano (110M, released July 2026, vendor claim of 3x realtime on 8 CPU cores), all MIT. Every Chatterbox output carries an imperceptible Resemble Perth watermark, which matters for the output-rights and disclosure design.

VoxCPM2 (Apache-2.0 code and weights, 2B, 48 kHz, 30 languages, clone and design, released 2026-04) is the only candidate TTS with official MPS support (--device auto) and also runs via llama.cpp-omni on Metal. That makes it the strongest commercially clean, Mac-runnable narration candidate. mlx-audio (MIT, community) also covers Qwen3-TTS, Kokoro, Chatterbox v2/v3 and VoxCPM2 on MLX.

VibeVoice TTS code was removed by Microsoft on 2025-09-05 and TTS-1.5B is marked 'Disabled'. The README says it is 'intended for research and development purposes only' even though the license is MIT. Drop it from the narration lane.

ElevenLabs now has Eleven v4 and v4 Turbo (eleven_v4, eleven_v4_turbo). List price is $0.08 and $0.04 per 1K characters, with a promo of $0.022 and $0.011 until Oct 12. ElevenLabs recommends v4 over v3, and neither v3 nor v4 supports SSML break tags. This changes the cost baseline for the Sabbath Echo business case: the switch-away savings should be computed against v4/Flash pricing, not historical v2/v3 spend.
